en: The Heart of the Middle Way composed by Bhavya;
the first chapter.
The non-abandonment of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is inconceivable, unknowable, without abode, and without characteristics;
it is indefinable, self-cognizable, without beginning or end, and auspicious. ||1||
It is free from conceptual construction, free from appearance, free from signs, and stainless;
it is neither dual nor non-dual, peaceful, and devoid of the movement of the intellect. ||2||
Homage be to that Teacher who, out of compassion, taught the reality that is beyond syllables by means of syllables; may he, whose speech is never false, be present in my heart. (3)

For those whose minds are fixed on great enlightenment through the initiation for the arising of the welfare of others, something is being stated according to my ability, in order to bring down the nectar of reality. (4)
Not abandoning the thought of awakening, relying upon the vows of the Sage, and seeking the knowledge of reality—this is the conduct for the accomplishment of all goals. (5)
Since bodhicitta is adorned with great loving-kindness, compassion, and primordial wisdom, and is the seed of the Buddhas, the wise should apply themselves to not abandoning it. ||6||
It is appropriate for one who is wise, great in being, unable to endure the suffering of others, who has correctly initiated vigor, and who is capable and virtuous. (7)
Having surveyed the entire world, which was obscured by the light of wisdom,
he himself crossed over the subterranean abyss of the impurities of saṃsāra in order to ferry others across.
Or what is the power of the Powerful One, that he [does not rescue] these helpless, wretched beings bound by the shackles of passion and the like within the terrible prison of saṃsāra? (9)
Having drunk the wine of negligence, they are fast asleep in the slumber of delusion,
their entire store of merit completely plundered by the thieves of discursive thoughts.
Though his bonds have been severed without remainder by the sharp sword of wisdom, he who is compassionate by nature does not remain liberated without liberating these beings. (11)
Even he who, alone and wretched, enjoys the meager pleasure born of desire acquired through the strength of his own arms— he too would be censured by the virtuous. (12)
How much more so for that which is difficult even for universal monarchs, Indras, and Brahmās to obtain—a common means, by way of method, that utterly severs craving? (13)

The nectar of realizing the true nature of reality is the complete pacification of all suffering; it is not overwhelmed by suffering and so forth, even up to the limit of the destruction of the body. (14)
Moreover, even toward those who are afflicted by suffering, I have previously caused them further pain through the obsession of the "grasps" of the afflictions, like applying salt to a wound. (15)
And for those who have been benefactors through love and great respect in other births, what other recompense could there be than leading them to nirvāṇa? (16)
The wise are not afflicted even by existences that are like flaming swords, for their minds are gladdened by the joy arising from accomplishing the welfare of others. (17)
Because it closes the doors to all miserable rebirths by refraining from immoral conduct, and because it destroys the activity of the afflictions through the practice of seeing emptiness. ||18||
Beholding the six realms of existence as if they were a pleasure-trip to a garden due to their merit, the virtuous feel no terror regarding the prison of saṃsāra. (19)

Because they perceive the faults of existence and because of their compassion, they do not abide in nirvāṇa; consecrated to the arising of the welfare of others, they remain and continue to abide in existence. ||20||
Because they do not perceive saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as either distinct or non-distinct, the wise do not abide anywhere, yet they are present everywhere in existence. //21//

Having attained the sovereignty of the wheel of the true Dharma—which is rich with the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment, a source of immeasurable virtues, and honored by gods and asuras—[he will become a Buddha]. (22)
Having filled the ten directions with fame and words as pure as the rays of the full autumn moon and as bright as pearls, [he departed]. (23)

Having established sons of noble character as mines of virtue—whose teachings are honored by the crest-jewels of gods, nāgas, and others—for the sake of maintaining the lineage of the Three Jewels. (24)
Because they have accomplished their own and others' tasks, they are at peace, most perfectly at peace;
others, however, are cut off through the severance of the aggregates, and they too are at peace.
A jackal is not capable of splitting the frontal globes of an intoxicated elephant;
nor is an elephant capable of protecting the circle of the earth bounded by the ocean.
In the presence of this mine of profound, unsurpassed, and noble qualities that transcend all calculation, a being of inferior capacity does not even desire the aspiration for Buddhahood. (27)
Who would not direct their mind toward the jewel-like qualities of the Perfectly Awakened One, which are immeasurable, marvelous, inconceivable, and surpass all radiance? (28)
Who, being a hero in performing the welfare of others through the deeds of a Great Being, would not remain even for an infinite saṃsāra as if it were but a single day? (29)

What accomplished person would not follow the path of the Noble Ones, whose sole activity is the welfare of others— a path which, even when transcended, becomes the very subject matter of their legends? (30)

Who would not bring this body—from which one makes oneself an instrument for accomplishing the welfare of others—to the solid essence of Mount Meru, rather than leaving it as insubstantial as a plantain tree or a bubble? (31)
At every moment, the fortunate one, out of compassion, transforms every basis of old age, death, and disease into a basis for the arising of the happiness of others. (32)
For this moment, in which the lamp of the true Dharma has been extinguished and the eight inopportune states have vanished,
must be made fruitful through the conduct of a Great Being. (33)
The first chapter, titled "Not Abandoning the Thought of Awakening":
Through noble deeds, one should remain in cyclic existence even for an infinite duration, as if it were but a single day. (29)
What successful person, even one who has transcended this world, would not follow the path of the Noble Ones, whose sole activity is the welfare of others—
this being the second chapter?
Taking refuge in the vow of the Sage, thus firmly undertaking great awakening for the welfare of the world,
he shines forth, having entered upon the fitting practice at every step. ||1||
With a loving-kindness that is unimpeded and a compassion that flows forth, he was never satiated by his realization of the true Dharma and was free from stinginess in the giving of the Dharma. ||2||
With a mind that is straightforward and free from pride, which perceives reality, which is blinded to seeing the faults of others, and which fears the occurrence of its own faults; (3)
Averse to disputes, social intercourse, and the Lokāyata philosophy, he was intent on instilling virtues even in those devoid of them, having cast aside all worldly attachment. ||4||
With a generosity born of compassion, he who has set his desire upon omniscience acts for the pacification of all suffering for the entire body of beings. (5)
Bathing in the pure waters of moral conduct, wearing the sacred thread of patience, bearing the mass of matted hair bound by vigor, he was devoted to meditation and wisdom. ||6||
With the eyes of his intellect wide open, he was adept in the knowledge of both the scriptures and the world; modesty and shame were his garments, and gentleness was the slender bond that held him.
He wears compassion as his black antelope skin; he carries the water-pot of faith;
he has the gates of his senses guarded by mindfulness; and he sits upon the cane seat of fortitude. ||8||
He dwells in the great and most delightful forest of asceticism that is the Mahāyāna;
his food is the fruit of the joy of meditative concentration, and his sphere of activity is the foundations of mindfulness. ||9||
Having cleansed his sins through the recitation of profound and sublime sūtras, he mutters the *sāvitrī* mantra of dependent origination by relying upon the two truths. (10)
Day after day, he worshipped the sun-like Samyaksambuddha with flowers of rich color that bloom at the beginning of each lunar phase and whose fragrance wafts in all directions.
Having sacrificed unwholesome intentions into the fire of analytical discernment, one should thus observe the vow of a sage for the attainment of the unsurpassed state. (12)

The second chapter, titled "Taking Refuge in the Vow of the Sage": Carrying a water-pot as pure as a *śraddhā*-berry, with the doors of his senses guarded by mindfulness, he sat upon a seat of cane-mat made of fortitude. (8)
He dwells in the great and most delightful forest of asceticism that is the Mahāyāna;
his nourishment is the fruit of the joy of meditative concentration, and his sphere of activity is the foundations of mindfulness. ||9||
Having cleansed his defilements through the recitation of profound and sublime sūtras, he mutters the *sāvitrī* mantra of dependent origination by relying upon the two truths. (10)
The third chapter, rich in colors,
is the "Seeking the Knowledge of Reality."
He whose eye consists of knowledge possesses true vision, and nothing else;
therefore, the wise person should be devoted to the pursuit of the knowledge of reality. ||1||
Even a blind man, if he possesses intelligence and desires to see, perceives objects that are distant,
subtle, or concealed, for his vision is unimpeded throughout the three worlds.
Even with a thousand eyes, one who lacks wisdom is blind,
because he cannot discern the true path to heaven and liberation from that which is not the path.
One whose eye has been opened by wisdom does not engage in giving and other such acts, which are like poisonous thorns—the longing for distinguished results, whether seen or unseen. ||4||
For one applies oneself to giving and the other perfections with the threefold purity;
out of compassion, for the sake of omniscience, yet with a mind that does not dwell even upon that. ||5||
Wisdom is the nectar that brings satisfaction, a lamp of unimpeded radiance,
the staircase to the palace of liberation, and the fire that consumes the fuel of the afflictions.
And that cognition, which is intended to be twofold in relation to the two truths, is so because it conforms to the discernment of conventional reality and ultimate reality. (7)

In the fulfillment of the two accumulations known as merit and wisdom—consisting of generosity and so forth—and in the definitive determination of their causes, fruits, relationships, characteristics, and so on. ||8||
The conventional wisdom should be understood as that which, based on the twelve sense-bases, practices great loving-kindness and compassion, and gathers and matures sentient beings. (9)
It effects the negation of the entire web of conceptual constructions;
it is peaceful, personally realized, non-conceptual, and beyond syllables. (10)
When reality is free from unity and plurality, like the stainless sky,
then wisdom that is both non-active and active becomes ultimate.
For it is not possible to ascend to the summit of the palace of reality without the ladder of correct conventional truth; therefore, [this must be accepted]. (12)
First, through conventional truth, one should become one whose mind is secluded;
thereafter, one becomes well-ascertained regarding the specific and general characteristics of phenomena. (13)
A wise person should apply themselves to the concentration of the mind, for that is the cause of the knowledge consisting of hearing and of all other forms of knowledge. (14)
Just as one does not see a face in turbid and agitated water, so too one does not perceive reality when the mind is uncollected and obscured by hindrances. //15//
Having bound the elephant of the mind to the pillar of the focal object with the rope of mindfulness,
one should gradually bring it under control by means of the goad of wisdom, as it wanders upon the wrong path.
One should pacify what is agitated by means of mental applications regarding impermanence;
one should expand what is contracted through the practice of vast objects of focus. (17)
One should withdraw the distracted mind by contemplating the defects of the objects that cause distraction;
one should also rouse the sunken mind by perceiving the benefits of vigor. (18)
One should wash away the unrestrained mind, stained by the mire of passion, hatred, and delusion, with the water of the contemplation of impurity, loving-kindness, and dependent origination. 19.
Having recognized it as secluded, immovable, peaceful, intent upon its object, workable, and pliant, one should maintain right equanimity therein. ||20||
With a concentrated mind, one should subsequently investigate with wisdom as follows:
"This intrinsic nature of phenomena which is apprehended through conventional usage," ||21||
But when investigated by the intellect, what is this in the ultimate sense? If it exists as such, then this alone is reality; if it is otherwise, then that [other] must be sought. (22)
One who is tormented by partiality can never attain peace;
[this applies to] all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned—the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements. (23)
They were taught for the Śrāvakas in order to eliminate the obscuration of afflictions;
for those whose nature is compassion, they were taught in order to eliminate the stains of both the afflictive and cognitive obscurations. (24)
Because it is the most gross, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is examined first;
even therein, the primary elements (bhūta) are examined first for the very reason already stated. (25)

In this regard, the elements such as earth and so forth do not possess an intrinsic nature from the perspective of ultimate reality, because they are produced, or because they possess causes and so forth, just like cognition. (26)
The earth does not have the nature of hardness because it is an element, just like wind;
supporting is not the function of the earth because it is produced, just like water. (27)
If the earth were considered to be of a solid nature and yet unreal even in reality,
then yogins would not be able to emerge from or sink into it. (28)
For those who meditate, the liquefaction of the earth is not possible through the power of meditation;
nor is its hardness lost, because its intrinsic nature is imperishable. (29)
In this way, it is not tenable that water, wind, and fire possess the intrinsic natures of fluidity and so forth, nor is their activity—namely cohesion, expansion, and digestion—tenable. (30)
For it is not accepted that wind and the other elements possess equal qualities conventionally, because they are perceived by the body-faculty or because they are elemental, just like earth. (31)
Earth and the other [elements] do not exist as substantial entities (*dravyasat*), because they are not perceived when their constituent parts of the causal complex are not perceived.
Whatever is not perceived in the manner described does not exist as a substantial entity, just like a forest. (32)
And this cognition of earth and so forth is not considered to have a substantially real object, because it has a cause or because it perishes, just like the cognition of a forest and the like. (33)

A sound that denotes [a universal] such as "earth" is not accepted as denoting a substance, because it is audible, just as a sound denoting [a collection] such as "army" is not accepted as denoting a substance. (34)
There is no inconclusiveness of the reason on account of the mind, mental factors, and cognitions;
for, like those [entities], their negation is likewise equivalent to the probandum. //35//

Palāśa, spandana, and other such trees are not desired as the originators of the forest, because they possess the properties of having causes and so forth, just like feet and other such [limbs]. ||36||
A forest as a composite whole (avayavin) is not considered to be composed of palāśa trees and the like,
because it is not fully present in each of them individually, just as [the whole] is not [present] in the hands and other limbs. //37//
Therefore, even the fault of the illustrative example (dṛṣṭāntadoṣa) does not apply to the thesis (pakṣa).
As to how it is also non-existent in the second case, that is now explained. ||38||
The word "forest" does not denote a collection of many indefinite substances, because it is the cause of a determinate cognition, like words such as "jar" or "bowl. (39)
For form is not apprehended by the visual faculty from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it is a composite, just like sound; or likewise, because it is derived from the elements. (40)
The eye does not perceive form, because it is composed of the elements (*bhautika*), just like its own nature;
or else, because it is the cause for the arising of pleasure and so forth, or because it is an object of verbal expression, just like taste and so forth. (41)

Likewise, one should characterize derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) as not [arising] from production [in the same way as fire and so forth], because of reasons such as its having a cause, or like the mind (*citta*). (42)
By this, whatever conceptualization of form has been imagined—characterized by color, shape, aggregation, and so forth, as well as the distinction between the subtle and the gross—is [refuted]. (43)
That which is prohibited must be understood according to its appropriate application;
this applies to the prohibition of sound, smell, taste, and touch.
This is the method. ||44||
From the perspective of ultimate reality, the visual faculty does not perceive form, because it is distinct from the mind and mental factors, just like the gustatory faculty. (45)

Alternatively, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the eye does not perceive form, because it lacks the nature of consciousness; since it is unproduced, it is like the skin and other sense organs. (46)
The visual faculty is not a translucent form whose object is color, because of reasons such as its being produced [by causes], with the skin and other [faculties] serving as examples. (47)

The eye is not considered to have form as its object, because it does not perceive its own nature, just like the auditory and other sense organs; or else, because it possesses the quality of being material (rūpitva), like taste and so forth. //48//
In the same way, for one who is not a seer, there is no seeing by means of sight;
or else, how could the seeing of form be possible for one whose nature is not that of a seer? (49)
Or how is it possible for that which is not of the nature of a seer to see form?
If the seer itself were the hearer, by what would its state of being a hearer be produced? (50)
Nor can omniscience and eternity be accepted [as attributes of God] because there is no specific reason to accept them;
nor can he be a single entity, because he possesses two distinct natures, like the body of another person. (51)

The visual faculty is not accepted as the instrument for the apprehension of form, because, while being devoid of mind, it is distinct from the seer, just like the auditory faculty and the others. (52)

Furthermore, its status as a seer is not tenable because it depends upon the eyes and other [senses], because it is subject to transformation like the mind, and likewise because of the arising of reflections. (53)
Since it is not seen by another sense organ, how can it possess the nature of a seer, like the mind?
In reality, the mind is not accepted as having the capacity to see forms, just as the self [is not]. (54)
Alternatively, because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) lacks substantial reality (*adravyasattva*), there is no seeing [of it], just as in that case;
or else, let there be agency (*kartṛtā*) due to the production of a distinct property (*dharmāntara*), like a bell. (55)
The eye is not logically like a ray of light because it is an organ of sense, like other organs;
for the visible object is the locus of the eyes of nocturnal creatures, whereas the eye itself is not visible. (56)
The eye does not have pleasure and so forth as its intrinsic nature, because it is a functional entity, just like a person;
nor is the eye omnipresent, because it exists [as a localized thing], just like its physical orb and so forth. ||57||
Alternatively: "Or, [the eye] exists for the sake of another because it is a mover toward all objects, just like a jar;
or, it is so because it is a cause for the perception of form, just like form. (58)
The eye is not conjoined with light, because it is a sense organ, like the skin and other organs;
nor is it composed of a preponderance of light, being essentially a refinement of the primary elements. (59)
The eye does not reach its object because it is a sense faculty, just like the mind;
or else, because it possesses form, or because it is a cause, or for that very reason [of being a sense faculty]. (60)

Because it grasps external objects directly and does not grasp the past or the future, the sense of smell and the others are not held to grasp objects that have already been reached, just like the eye. (61)
And because there is a negation of what is equivalent to the probandum, there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason] due to skin and so forth;
by this method, it should be understood that hearing and the rest have also been refuted.
The triad characterized by the mind, the ear, and the eye does not reach its object, because they are sense-faculties, just like the nose; or else, because they are the causes of consciousness. (63)
They are to be understood through vision alone, according to the detailed explanation already given;
[for] the faculties of hearing, smelling, tasting, and touch are excluded. (64)
The same method of negation applies to sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles as well.
The wise,
with an impartial mind,
should understand this as appropriate. 65.
Feeling, whose nature is the experience [of objects], is not tenable from the perspective of ultimate truth, because it is associated with consciousness, just like the other mental factors. (66)
That which is pleasant and beneficial is not accepted [as pleasure] because it is born of contact, like anything else;
by the aforementioned reason, it should be understood that what is painful and of the nature of affliction is not [pleasure]. (67)
Likewise, the sensation that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant is [unreal] because it has thirst as its fruit, just like the other two;
or else, because its nature as consciousness is denied in the intended sense. ||68||
By this, perception is explained; and the formative forces (saṃskāras) consist of both.
The wise should understand them as appropriate through an impartial mind. (69)
In reality, the mind does not have the nature of cognizing objects, because it possesses an objective support, like perception, or because it is perishable, like a lamp. (70)
By that teaching of the words of the proof which analyzes the five aggregates,
By means of the aggregates, the elements are to be known, and the sense-bases are likewise to be known. ||71||

Arising and the other [characteristics] are not logically possible as the defining marks of the conditioned, because that which is characterized is itself conditioned and is to be understood [as such], just like anything else. (72)
Nor is it held that things possess a self-nature (sātmatā) simply because their defining characteristics exist;
for a reason might otherwise be contradictory or its meaning unestablished. (73)
Hardness is the characteristic of earth; it is not joined with "earth-ness" [as its essence].
Since it is the cause of body-consciousness, how could it be the characteristic of fire? (74)
By the very definition of being an ox,
one does not desire its hump and dewlap.
Because it is analyzed by a superior cognition,
just like, for example, the definition of a donkey. //75//
If they were one, how could there be characteristics? For it would not characterize reality itself.
Otherwise, how could there be a characteristic?
For one thing does not perceive another as "otherness. //76//

In the ultimate sense, no going is perceived in that which has already gone, because it is a past time-period (adhvan) or because going is absent; just as in the case of something other than that which has already gone. //77//

Because that which is being traversed cannot be established as distinct from what has been traversed and what has not yet been traversed, motion is not known to exist in the process of being traversed from the perspective of ultimate reality. (78)
Furthermore, even when that which is being traversed is inexpressible as either "gone" or "not yet gone," there is no motion,
because it is a temporal path (*adhvan*), just like the past path or the future path. (79)
Since motion is not established, there is no goer; nor is it accepted that non-motion goes.
Motion is not possible for one who is not a goer, because of the absence of motion, just as previously [stated]. (80)
The notion that "it moves" is held to arise from its own nature when there is a connection with another object;
it is not like [the notion of] "one with a staff," because there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) and because the cognition and the word persist [even when the action ceases]. //81//

The delusion of movement, like that of a flame and so forth, is based on a continuous stream of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arising in successive directions; it is conventional (*sāṃvṛtī*), not real in the ultimate sense (*tattvataḥ*). ||82||

Because the aggregate lacks substantiality, or else because it is devoid of activity, it is not logically tenable for the followers of Kapila to conceive of it as a mover from the perspective of ultimate reality. (83)

If the collection is substantially real, it is untenable because it cannot be apprehended when its constituents are not apprehended—just like the nature of those [constituents] themselves—since they lack substantial existence. (84)
Even though this is a refutation of all remaining [theoretical] activities, this direction has been set forth:
if intrinsic nature is desired because of the real existence of saṃsāra, liberation, and so forth, [then it must be refuted]. (85)
When their form, as it has been conceptualized, is no longer apprehended, then, having analyzed forms, from where and how could there be bondage and liberation? (86)

However, these two are applicable to things that lack intrinsic nature, which are like illusions and dreams, having acquired their specific identities through the power of their own causes and conditions. (87)

The transmigration of name-and-form is not tenable from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it is conditioned, just as the transmigration of external things such as earth and so forth is not accepted. (88)

Name-and-form is not liberated in any way from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it possesses origination or because it is subject to destruction, just like external things such as water and so forth. (89)
In reality, neither a person transmigrates nor is liberated;
for it is a mere designation, like a house, or because it is something that can be expressed, like a fragrance. (90)
Or, conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are devoid of a person (niṣpudgala), because they possess causes, just like a jar;
or because they possess origination, because they are subject to destruction, or because they are objects of cognition, just like a clod of earth. ||91||

Because it is substantially existent yet inexpressible [as either identical to or different from its qualities], the person (pudgala) is held to be like fragrance; for there would be doubt regarding it as being like the son of a barren woman, who is likewise inexpressible as being dark or fair.
Thus, the aggregates are selfless, devoid of a living soul, and bereft of a sentient being;
[this is seen] by the wise with a mind of equanimity.
This should be understood according to what is appropriate. //93//
The aggregate of body and sense-faculties is considered to be without a self in reality, because it possesses causes, just like a pillar, or because it is a composite, like a heap of grain. (94)
If the existence of the self is asserted on the grounds of such causes as memory, recognition, and the arising of cognition, those reasons would be unestablished (*asiddha*). 95.

If it is thus sought to be established that "the body possesses sense-faculties and a self," then the reasons would be non-common (asādhāraṇa) due to the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya). //96//
Just as this word "self" (ātman) is used in some cases according to its literal meaning, while in others it is used figuratively—
just as the word "lion" [is used for a man]— if that were so, the self would not be established [as a real entity]. (97)
Now, if it is argued that the object of consciousness is established as being real elsewhere,
then there would be a contradiction due to its opposition to [the properties of] permanence, omnipresence, and so forth. (98)
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, bondage and liberation are not desired for anyone.
Just as with what has been traversed, what has not been traversed, and what is being traversed, so too should the rest of the mind be explained.

For when the mind has arisen and is facing toward its own destruction, then for whom and by what is passion desired? One who is impassioned is not desired [as such], for he is already destroyed. ||100||

If that which is being born is held to be affected [by passion], then how can it be so if it is not yet oriented toward birth? For that which is unborn, such a connection with an action lacking a substratum is not admitted. (101)
They are without attachment even to that which cannot be described as being in the process of arising, already arisen, or unarisen.
Even though it is inexpressible, because of its inexpressibility, the mind is not possessed of passion, just as passion itself is not.

If it is maintained that the mind becomes "attached" by taking on the form of the capacity [of attachment], then, like the cognition of a red crystal, how could there be the cognition of that [mind] as being itself red? (103)
Thus, because there is an absence of passion, the conceptualization of passion is merely conventional. One should understand all phenomena accordingly, just like passion itself. (104)

It is logical that an entity (bhāva) must have a substance (dravya) as its substratum; and since that [entity] is not distinct from it, it follows for you that there would be no passion even in the mind, just as there is none in passion itself. (105)

It is not logical for passion to be something other [than the impassioned one], because it cannot be apprehended when the impassioned one is not apprehended. Even if there were separateness, as in the case of the self of the impassioned one, there would be no state of being impassioned, just as with anything else. (106)
There is no distinction in the mind arising from passion with respect to the cognition of an object;
for the object and other factors are the same, and there is no other cause for such a distinction. (107)
Therefore, the designation of a collection by means of a single constituent is accepted as being dependent upon its own production, just as [one speaks of] a tree when it has blossomed. (108)
Because of the abandonment of that [duality], nirvāṇa is not tenable,
since it would follow that it is neither an entity nor a non-entity in the ultimate sense.
It is not a defining characteristic. //109//
If nirvāṇa were indeed an entity, then because it is an entity, it would be conditioned;
and because it is conditioned, it would be subject to its opposite, just like the cessation of the conditioned. (110)
If non-existence, by virtue of being non-existent, were dependent on another because it is perishable,
then this [non-existence] would not be accepted as the counter-position,
just like perishability which is dependent on another. ||111||
This [self], even if unconditioned, is untenable due to the refutations stated previously;
furthermore, what distinction is there between this and the liberated self postulated by the Sāṃkhya? (112)
The afflictions perish of their own accord, arising from the fire-sticks of conceptual construction;
since they are not accumulated, for whom could there be liberation through their destruction?
May your liberation be indestructible. (113)
Since that which is unarisen likewise lacks existence, the principle [of liberation] is the same as that of conceptual construction.
Tell me, through the destruction of what is there liberation—of something perishable or even of something imperishable? (114)

Through the awakening to the emptiness of intrinsic nature and the cessation of even that cognition, one attains the state of inexhaustible dharmas and the inexhaustible through the yoga of non-attainment. (115)
Those who seek their own welfare and investigate things as they truly are do not resort to these words;
for from them come the foul-smelling eructations of the disease of wrong views. (116)
Its existence is not tenable because of the existence of cognitive distortions;
since its conceptualization is similar to that of passion, it too is merely conventional.
How much more so, since the intrinsic nature of mind and mental factors has already been refuted:
passion does not exist by way of its own nature as passion, nor is that [object] colored by it. (118)
By this, one should understand that hatred, delusion, and so forth are likewise refuted;
and thus, because bondage is not established, the absence of intrinsic nature is unshakable. (119)
In ultimate reality, the earth is not different from my own self,
because it possesses causes, just like wind, or because it is a real entity, just like consciousness. (120)
In ultimate reality, no water is perceived apart from the earth;
because it possesses the nature of arising, just as the self is not separate from the earth, so too is water not separate from the earth. (121)

Nor is there a difference in the nature of earth and the other elements based on the differences in their sounds or cognitions, nor based on a difference in their characteristics as effects, because [in either case] they would lack connection with the property to be proven.
Furthermore, because there is the designation "the self of form" even though there is no difference [between them], doubt arises;
and since that which is being conceptualized is unestablished, this [reason] would have an unestablished object. (123)
Therefore, even though [the object] is divided by distinctions such as sound and so forth, those [reasons] are deviant,
even when the qualifiers are stated.
are likewise prevented by an adversary. ||124||
The state of being both [identical and different] is impossible due to contradiction, just as fire cannot possess both heat and cold;
or rather, that [position] is also untenable because it has been refuted in the arguments concerning the positions of identity and difference. (125)
Even though everything consists of two natures, the well-known part serves as the illustration.
Therefore, the deficiency of the example does not arise with respect to the opponent. ||126||
And its establishment is relative and imagined through the conceptualization of desire;
it is not established because neither of the two, nor even one of them, is previously established. ||127||
In all dualistic doctrines, this same method applies even to negation;
thus, by the procedure already explained, intrinsic nature is refuted. (128)
Thus these conditioned phenomena have been examined by way of a thousandfold analysis.
The unconditioned consists of the two cessations, as well as space and suchness. (129)
For analytical cessation is not an entity from the perspective of ultimate reality, because its nature is eternal and unchanging, like the form of the son of a barren woman. (130)
Because it is unarisen, because it is non-differentiated, or again because it is not an effect;
or else because it is not included among the conditioned, and also because its cessation is impossible. ||131||
Furthermore, that which is considered the effect for something is certainly not its cause, because it has not yet arisen and for other such reasons, like the horn on the head of an elephant. (132)

It is determined that an effect whose cause has not arisen is not accepted [as such], because it is an effect; for example, a small thing [like a sprout] does not have a sky-flower or the like as its cause. (133)
By this, the wise person should understand that space, suchness, the directions, time, the self, and so forth—whatever is unconditioned—is likewise refuted. (134)
Whatever is postulated by non-Jain teachers—such as substance, the primary principle, the soul, and so forth—is to be refuted, as appropriate, by those who are experts in logic and scripture. (135)

Thus, having contemplated the selflessness of entities—which, according to one's own or others' tenets, is conceived as having a self—the wise person, having discerned this, should drink the nectar of the knowledge of reality. (136)
Alternatively, the expansion of the web of conceptual construction, beginning with such [thoughts], based on things that have arisen, forcibly agitates the ignorant. (137)
The wise one examines things as they truly are by means of the lamp of knowledge;
through the negation of birth and the consequent pacification thereof, there is then the cessation of conceptual proliferation. (138)
In that regard, first of all, arising from itself is not tenable even conventionally;
because it would possess its own self-nature, just as the arising of curd from itself does not exist. (139)
Entities do not arise from their own selves because they are entities, just like a person;
nor does a self exist for those things that have not yet arisen, because they are unarisen, like a flower in the sky. (140)

Even if you maintain that the sky and so forth are what is expressed by the term "the absence of a sky-flower," we have no deficiency in our position because [we do not claim] that it is a sky-flower. (141)
If it is argued that the cause of an effect is its own self, and therefore its birth is considered to be from that [self],
and thus the birth of entities is held to be from themselves; 142.
Because it is non-different from itself, the cause would be a non-cause;
and because it is unproduced, what could be the cause of what, or what could be a non-cause? (143)
If the self exists as a real entity, the postulation of a cause for that entity is futile;
therefore, it must have arisen from that very [self], resulting in the identity of the producer and the produced. (144)
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because milk persists in the form of curd,
then it is not the case that there is no contradiction regarding the father, since he does not persist in the form of the son. (145)
Because the opposing side is impossible, the reason is not considered contradictory;
thus, first of all, the self-arising of entities is not tenable. (146)
Furthermore, since intrinsic nature is impossible, who can be considered other than whom, and for what reason?
A horse's horn is not regarded as "other" than the state of being a mountain peak or a cow's horn. (147)

From the perspective of ultimate reality, the eyes and other [senses] are not conditions that produce visual consciousness, because they are "other" [than it], just like vīraṇa grass and the like. (148)

The cognition of form is not held to have the intended eye and so forth as its cause, because it is other [than them], or because it does not exist prior [to them], just like jars, cloths, and the like. (149)
The otherness of that which is unborn is merely conventional and not real;
thus, it is understood that arising from another is likewise untenable. (150)
The arising of that which is inexpressible is purposeless once it has arisen;
nor can there be birth for that which is unborn, because, like a sky-flower, it lacks the nature of being born. (151)
Furthermore, regarding the arising of that which is currently being born, the same objection applies;
for even that which is inexpressible cannot arise, because it is inexpressible, just like anything other than it. (152)
In reality, the eye and the other [senses] are empty of an imagined nature, because they are produced or because they are subject to destruction, just like water created by illusion. (153)
Because it is negated as being equivalent to the probandum, there is no doubt that it is not of another nature;
for even though it is unconstructed, its illusory nature is considered false from the perspective of ultimate reality. (154)
Because it is the cause for the conceit of being one's own self, this imagined nature is established through its perceived aspect; thus, we do not suffer from a deficiency in our example. (155)
For the eye and the other [senses] are empty of intrinsic nature in reality, because they are produced or because they are subject to destruction, like a Buddha created by Māra. (156)
And whatever is the intrinsic nature of entities, that nature does not exist in reality,
because it is produced, just like the heat of water or its stability. (157)
For the arising of entities by themselves is not tenable;
nor is arising through another entity observed, as a cow does not arise from the nature of a donkey. (158)
And birth from external conditions such as causes and so forth is merely conventional;
therefore, there is no contradiction with what has been accepted, because those [conditions] do not exist in reality. (159)
A condition is not logically tenable for that which exists or for that which does not exist, because of its being both existent and non-existent;
or, like something other than those, since it is unproduced, how can there be a condition? (160)

A cause does not produce an effect because it is empty of that [effect], just like anything else; nor does it do so by virtue of being produced from it, because what is about to arise does not exist prior [to its production], just like anything else. ||161||
This [cause] does not produce what is unarisen, what is currently arising, or what has already arisen;
because of the faults already stated and because of the non-arising [of such things], therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no cause.
For that which has already arisen, there is no connection with an object of cognition; therefore, arising for what has already arisen is futile.
Furthermore, for that which has not yet arisen, there is no arising because it is unarisen, just like that which possesses the nature of non-arising. ||163||
For that which is being born, there must be conjunction; and that [conjunction] does not occur without an objective support (ālambana).
It is not accepted that the entry into the action of birth can belong to that which lacks its constituent parts. ||164||

Alternatively, it is not accepted that mind and mental factors have an object of perception (ālambana) in reality, because they are produced [from themselves] or because they are the grasped, just like form. (165)
Furthermore, for that which possesses an object, [the relationship] would be impossible due to a difference in time;
and since that [object] is non-existent, in the absence of an object, what could be the object of what? (166)
There is no cessation of that which has not arisen, because it is unarisen like a flower in the sky;
nor is there cessation in that which has already ceased.
It does not exist because it has ceased, just as in the case of one who is dead. ||167||
It is not [produced] when [the cause] has ceased, because it would then be non-existent, like a present lamp;
nor is it accepted [to be produced] while it is ceasing, due to the refutation already stated above. (168)
Even so, it would have to be simultaneous [with its cause], or it might even be at a different time;
for it is logical that it exists while in the process of ceasing, like the final mind of an Arhat. (169)
Since birth does not exist in reality, the existence of an entity is not tenable;
therefore, like the existence of the son of a barren woman, it is not considered to be a dominant condition. (170)
Whether empty or non-empty of its effect, the condition becomes the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
It is not empty because of its emptiness, just as the cognition of sound [is not empty] of the eye. //171//
Even conventionally, it is not non-empty, because dependent origination is the subverting proof;
furthermore, for you, an effect would not be an effect, or else that which is non-existent would become an effect. (172)
If the causal capacity itself is the effect, what else could be the cause?
For the relationship of container and contained is not admitted for that which is non-different from it. (173)
Or, it may be merely a synonym for the effect, just as "space" [is used] regarding the presence of space;
when that is the case, what is its cause, by which it is held to be non-empty? (174)
Since that which exists lacks origination, what can be considered the sovereign of what?
Since that which does not exist lacks conditions, what can be considered the sovereign of what? (175)

If it is argued that jars and other things are seen to have been produced, and thus the reason [for their being unproduced] is useless because it is contradicted by the perception of what is seen— then such contradiction by perceived cognition indeed serves as a sublation.
The birth of jars and other such things is perceived by the common intellect of the ignorant;
this negation is not likewise [perceived by that intellect], and therefore the fault previously mentioned does not apply. (177)
In reality, there is no cognition having form as its object that is self-cognized;
for since such [cognition] does not arise, its sublation cannot be a sublater. (178)

Perceptual cognition is not at all established as being in accordance with reality from the perspective of ultimate truth, because it is distinguished by the intellect of the ignorant, like the cognition of a wheel [produced by] a firebrand. (179)

Nor is the object within its range [the self], because it is conditioned, just like the cognition of a self; and since form and so forth lack substantial reality, our perception does not constitute a sublation. ||180||
Furthermore, direct perception does not subvert the investigation of the conduct of the wise;
nor is the word of those blinded by the cataract of ignorance entitled to authority regarding reality. (181)
Even for that which already exists, birth is not desired; what could birth possibly bring to that which already exists?
If you say it results in grossness, then the effect is not pre-existent, because grossness was impossible prior [to its production]. (182)

Furthermore, that grossness which belongs to the eye is not produced by its own causal conditions, because it did not previously exist, just like a jar; or else, because it is an object of cognition, just like an enjoyer. (183)
And since, in general, according to conventional truth, we accept that which is intended as the enjoyer and so forth,
no fault regarding the example arises here in any respect. (184)
If it is argued that there is no fault because of manifestation, then what is manifested by what?
For example, as a jar is manifested by a lamp; yet manifestation does not belong to that which already exists. (185)
Even conventionally, by means of a lamp, a jar is made to be accompanied by illumination; or else, the cognition of it is produced, or even the arising of its opposite.
That which is unmanifested is not manifested because of its lack of manifestation, like a flower in the sky;
or, according to their own doctrine, they might point to the enjoyer and the primary matter (pradhāna) as examples. (187)
Nor is the enjoyer omnipresent, nor is he a conscious being without a cause;
for if he were so, his manifestation and his unmanifest state would both be lost. (188)
Furthermore, if that which is the effect is admitted by you to be the Pradhāna itself,
then since it exists in the form of both the manifest (vyakta) and the primal matter (pradhāna),
how could there be no modification? (189)

Those activities which are the manifestors of something are not considered to be its manifestors, because they possess the nature of causes and so forth, just as threads and the like are not manifestors of curd. (190)

If it is argued that [the example] is deficient because the capacity for that [cognition] is also present in threads and the like, we say no; for in their state as threads and so forth, they do not manifest that [capacity]. (191)

Arising from itself, from another, or from both is not accepted, nor does it arise from that which is both existent and non-existent; for the doctrine of both has already been examined and found untenable through reasoning. (192)

Even conventionally, it is not accepted that an effect is manifested by its conditions, because [the effect] conforms to the differences of those [conditions], just as a jar [conforms] to clay and so forth. (193)
For even conventionally, it is not accepted that the eye arises without a cause;
this is because it is connected with [its causes] both generally and specifically, like a bowl. (194)
One should characterize [the conditioned] by its being an effect, its arising in succession, its perishability, its transformation, the regularity of causes and conditions, and its genus. ||195||

If it is argued that a *śivaka* (a protuberance) is not considered to have arisen because it has ceased to be a different kind of entity—just as a jar [does not arise] because it is perishable or because it is an effect; //196//
Just as a pit is not produced when it has already ceased to exist in the form of a pit,
if you accept that the "shikhara" (the peak) is likewise [produced],
then exactly what you desire is established. (197)
Furthermore, if the cause is thus contradictory because its causal efficiency has ceased,
then if it were argued that this occurs through a continuum (*saṃtati*) of what has not yet perished, there would indeed be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāritā*).
Prior to the first cognition of the embryo and so forth, there exists a cognition that has just ceased;
because it differs according to the difference in its objects, or because it is a cognition, just like the cognitions occurring after that. (199)

The cognition of sound and the cognition of form that arise in Caitra—there can be no identity between these two because their objects are distinct, just as in the case of cognitions belonging to different mental continua. (200)

The impossibility of an example for that [cognition] does not arise from the oneness of cognition, nor does its oneness follow from its being a cognition, because that is subject to deviation by another cognition. (201)
If it is argued by the nihilists that the dying-consciousness of a fool is without rebirth-linking because it is a dying-consciousness,
like the final consciousness of an Arhat; [202]

The reason might be inconclusive because of the mind at the moment of death in the past, since there exists the recollection of former births and so forth; and that [mind] is indeed real according to the principle already stated. (203)

The mind at the moment of death is indeed productive of another state of consciousness, just as the mind of a non-noble person, being accompanied by ignorance, is productive of that [subsequent] mind. (204)
The body, the senses, and the intellect are not desired [to be the self], as they are produced by one's own karma;
because they are perishable, like a pot. Therefore, if you say that there is no other world, [you are mistaken]. (205)

Since that [body] is not produced by that very [self], nor is it produced by anything other than it, what indeed is our concern here in regard to the claim that "the body is not produced by the karma of another"? (206)
Furthermore, there exists no illustrative example for [growth] being produced without action; the arising of trees and so forth occurs through the power of the karma of sentient beings. (207)
Just as weapons grow in the realms of hell and wish-fulfilling trees grow in the higher realms.
And how can the intellect be so utterly distinct from the elements? (208)
Consciousness arises in insentient elements, just like the power of intoxication [in fermented grain], or like fire from a sun-crystal, because they possess the nature of being born. (209)
Because the power of intoxication is insentient, your example is deficient;
furthermore, because the cause belongs to a different class, your reason is also contradictory. ||210||
It is not perceived that the internal elements are cognizers, because they have the nature of solidity and so forth, and because they are [mere] elements, just like other [external] elements. (211)

Therefore, the consciousness at conception and so forth must be understood by the wise as being preceded by another consciousness, because it possesses the nature of a grasper, just like the consciousnesses that follow it. (212)
An infant seeks nourishment due to the practice performed in a previous life, just as one whose faculties are fully developed moves about for the sake of food. (213)
The reason is not inconclusive on account of magnets, stones, and the like;
nor is it unestablished, because the ingestion of such food is observed. (214)
The world is not created by God, because it is the cause of pleasure for someone;
just as one who produces pleasure is not himself created by God. (215)
Because it is either causeless or unborn, God is not the cause of the universe;
just as a flower in the sky is not accepted as the cause of the universe. (216)
The Supreme Lord is not the ultimate cause of this entire world, because He possesses a mind, just as a cowherd is not the ultimate cause of the world. (217)
Since the existence of things arises from a causal complex, there is no single entity, nor is there a Lord (Īśvara);
nor is anything produced by a single creator. Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness [in this argument]. ||218||
If the eye and other sense organs are held to possess a Lord because they are many, like servants,
then the Lord would be their opposite, since he is established as being unborn and singular.
Alternatively, [the world] is desired to have an agent because it is a created thing, like a pot and so forth.
If you mean that there is an agent whose specific nature is not specified, then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Furthermore, there can be no positive concomitance (anvaya) with those [entities] characterized by such qualities as being eternal, unitary, and subtle;
moreover, that [universal] would incur the defects of being non-eternal, material, and produced.

If it is argued that karma is the sovereign cause of the diversity of the world, comprising both sentient beings and their environments, then one is merely proving what is already established by conventional truth. (222)
By this [same reasoning], one should refute the claims that time, the primal person (puruṣa), primordial matter (pradhāna), atoms, or even Viṣṇu are the cause of this world. ||223||

If it is claimed that the arising of a Buddha is for the purpose of destroying the darkness of false views, and likewise the arising of the sense-bases [is for the same purpose], this is an untenable reply. (224)
Since there is no temporal path and no arising, for what and what kind of view is it intended?
It is the agency of the arising of a Buddha for the sake of awakening to that which has not [previously] come into being. (225)
If the asura were not other than the sura, how could there be such impermanence?
If the asura were other than the sura, how could non-interruption be logical? (226)
Even if it were inexpressible, like a jar, how could there be an avoidance of annihilation?
Even if Nirvana were both existent and non-existent, there would be no transcending of the other [extreme]. ||227||
If there is arising of that which has already ceased, how is it not eternalism?
If there is no arising of that which has ceased, how is it not the doctrine of annihilationism? (228)
Because the continuum is not a substantial entity, why would there be annihilation or permanence?
Due to the absence of that [continuum], non-arising is logical, which is neither annihilation nor permanence. ||229||
The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma is for the sake of the non-arising of suffering;
therefore, if arising were intended because of the existence of that fruit [of the teaching], [it would contradict their intent]. (230)
As before, since that [result] does not arise, of what is non-arising asserted?
Non-arising is not its result; rather, the thorough knowledge of it is its result. (231)
Because it is not produced by that very [action], it is not logical that it be self-made;
nor is it accepted as made by another, because one thing cannot be joined with the action of another. (232)
Suffering arising from one's own continuum is not accepted [as the self], because of the impossibility of [the self as] a sentient being and so forth;
nor is that suffering [the self] because it lacks substantiality and because there is no distinction [between them], nor is suffering the continuum itself. (233)
If, in reality, the conditioned phenomena such as the eye and so forth are purified because they are designated by the term "sentient being," just like a Buddha; (234)
The Buddha does not have the nature of arising, nor is he non-arising; likewise, his manifestation is not from that [nature].
Alternatively, because he lacks intrinsic existence, his appearance may be like the self or like an illusion. (235)

Form is not the Buddha because it is an object of awakening and because it arises [and perishes], like a clod of earth; nor is consciousness the Buddha, because its nature consists of the appearance of other things, like a magical illusion. (236)
The Buddha is not the material aggregates, for he is not considered to be comprised of the aggregates;
this is because [the aggregates] possess the nature of arising and passing away, or else because they are objects of knowledge, like form. (237)
Furthermore, because of the fault of destruction upon the destruction of those [aggregates], it is not logical that the Buddha is the aggregates;
nor is he other than them, because of the absence of distinct characteristics, like a self—how then could he exist for us? (238)
That which is non-substantial and non-existent is held to be inexpressible, as previously refuted;
or, like a jar, because it is inexpressible, how can its state of being "Buddha" be maintained? (239)
Because one who perceives dependent origination sees the Perfectly Awakened One, the arising of the sense-bases is not accepted [as real], since that [arising] has been refuted as before. (240)
It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither from both existence and non-existence, nor from the eternal, nor from no cause;
it is neither from this nor from that, being free from the extremes of permanence and annihilation. (241)
Since arising is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, what kind of arising is it?
How, then, can the vision of that Teacher be understood through vision? (242)

The doctrine of those who maintain the existence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is self-defeating; however, for one for whom arising is like the arising of an illusion, it is logically consistent. (243)

Because the stains of the aforementioned faults have been removed and because the torch of the true Dharma has been illuminated, the conventional perception of the Buddha occurs in the form of ritual action and assistance. (244)
Because it is like an illusion and is not real, its demonstration according to ultimate reality is inconceivable, unknowable, indefinable, and beyond illustration. //245//
For one who perceives that which is signless, appearance-less, non-conceptual, and beyond syllables—the intellect and the object of cognition—that perception is [in truth] non-perception. (246)
Thus, in the ultimate sense, it does not arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause; it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor otherwise. (247)
No entity whatsoever arises or is manifested in any way from causes such as Keśava, Īśa, Puruṣa, Pradhāna, or atoms. (248)
In that regard, there is the reliance upon intrinsic nature, activity, the characterized and the characteristic, and the basis for identity, difference, affliction, purification, and action. (249)
Just as a lash of a whip, a variegated painting, or seeds do not grow in space, so too are all conceptual constructions in this [reality]. (250)
Just as one with pure and stainless eyes, upon the removal of cataracts, does not perceive [illusory] hair, mosquitoes, double moons, or sunbeams; //251//

Just so, when the darkness and cataracts of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable have been removed, the wise one, possessing the stainless eye of perfect knowledge, does not perceive anything at all. (252)
Just as one who is fast asleep might see sons, wives, celestial chariots, palaces, and so forth by the power of supernatural accomplishment, yet does not see them upon waking; ||253||

In the same way, one whose eye of intelligence has been opened, having awakened through the cessation of the sleep of ignorance, no longer perceives those things previously apprehended by conventional truth. (254)
Just as one sees non-existent beings in the darkness at night,
one does not see them even when the sun has risen and one's eyes are wide open. 255.
The wise one does not perceive the domain of the mind and mental factors, having utterly destroyed all latent impressions of ignorance by means of the light of perfect knowledge. (256)

Because their intrinsic nature is unestablished or because they are unborn by way of intrinsic nature, one does not perceive the existence of an intrinsic nature in entities, as they are like an illusion. (257)

Because they possess origination from the perspective of conventional reality, or else because they possess causes, one does not perceive an existent intrinsic nature in things, for they are like illusions. (258)

Nor is the cognition that "entities do not exist" considered to be in accordance with reality, because it has ceased through the gateway of conceptual construction, like the perception of a man in a tree stump. (259)

Alternatively, the nature of an entity is considered false when it is perceived by a cognition of what is non-existent, because it is accessible to conceptual cognition, like the cognition of water in a mirage. (260)

In this very way, through the negation of both existence and non-existence, as well as of the intellect and the object of cognition, the non-conceptual wisdom of the wise arises by means of the yoga of non-birth. (261)
Because all phenomena are empty, or even because they are not non-empty, a non-conceptual cognition is not desired; for, as before, that [conceptualization] is what is being negated. (262)
Since emptiness is indeed empty by its very nature as emptiness and so forth, the wise person does not perceive even emptiness as "emptiness. (263)

Even though it is devoid of appearance and is the nature of reality, being the object of non-conceptual cognition, it is not "as-it-is" because it is an object of apprehension, just as the perception of the moon in water is not the actual moon. (264)

Even non-conceptual cognition, though its object is the non-conceptual reality, is false because its intrinsic nature consists of [the realization of] selflessness and so forth, just like conceptual cognition. (265)
Since the object of knowledge is in every way unestablished, that wherein even non-conceptual cognition does not arise—those who know reality recognize that as the incomparable reality. (266)
Because of the awakening to that, he is called "Buddha," who is the non-arising of the intellect;
he is the primary [awakening] through the awakening to non-awakening, due to the total destruction of conceptual construction and dream. (267)

Either through the culmination of the knowable and so forth, or through the awakening to equality, or by means of emanations for the sake of awakening the lotuses of those capable of liberation; ||268||
Without producing or ceasing phenomena that are distinct in character, one attains equality through equanimity, or the equality of oneself and others. (269)

Because he has attained perfect awakening without any object of apprehension in this world of men and gods, he is called "the Fully Awakened One" (Saṃbuddha) precisely because of his awakening to non-awakening. (270)
Just as the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains such whether things are added or removed, so too has he gone; therefore, he is the Tathāgata. ||271||
One must go everywhere without exception, free from extremes and partiality; for the Sugata is the "Well-Gone" because, even through the movement of the body, there is no going. //272//

It is immeasurable because it is to be awakened to as immeasurable; it is also incalculable because it cannot be grasped; it is inconceivable because it is not accessible to the mind; and it is non-demonstrable—
Because of the illustration. ||273||
It is indefinable because it cannot be defined as "this" or "that" in any way;
it is stainless due to the absence of defilement, and auspicious because of the cessation of all afflictions.

In every respect, because it is free from conceptual construction and devoid of appearance, and because its nature is such, it is said to be eternal due to its eternity; and it is eternal because it accomplishes its purpose eternally. //275//
It is peaceful because it is empty of intrinsic nature; it is signless because it lacks intrinsic nature; and it is also signless by virtue of not approaching any signs. //276//
For it is signless because it is without appearance;
indeed, by virtue of being without appearance, it is signless and without appearance for those whose nature is compassion and who desire to see it. (277)
It is non-abiding because it is selfless; it is free from conceptual construction because it does not abide;
it is free from proliferation.
Because it is conceptual, it is without an objective support, since that [object] is not apprehended. ||278||
It is without arising, without form, without change, and luminous;
it is equal to the unequal, limitless, non-conceptual, and without characteristics. ||279||
Those whose pure eyes consist of dwelling in the state of non-conceptualization and effortless spontaneity perceive that Great Being as being like space, through the very absence of seeing. (280)
Even those who have transcended verbal expressions such as salutation and mental attention—
homage be to them from the heart, for they pay homage to the Protector. (281)

Because it is superposed with the reasoning of the Buddhas and so forth, because it conforms to practice, and because it is entirely free from conceptual construction, it is held to be inexpressible in its true nature. (282)
Here words turn back; this is not the domain of the mind. Conceptualization ceases, and the silence of knowledge arises. (283)

This is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas—those who possess an infinite mass of merit and who know the immeasurable objects of knowledge; it is the auspicious cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). (284)
He is not visible to the fleshly eye, nor is he visible to the divine eye;
even by means of knowledge that is both conceptual and non-conceptual, he is difficult to perceive. (285)
Like heaven to the evil-minded, like freedom from conflict to those who seek it, and like the sun to those born blind, [the Truth] is beyond the reach of logicians. ||286||
It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; it is not other than these, nor is it otherwise.
It is neither minute, nor great, nor one; it is neither far away, nor even near. (287)
Nothing whatsoever arises from this in any way, nor is anything manifested;
nothing at all abides herein, nor does anything dissolve. (288)
This is that supreme Brahman which is not grasped even by Brahmā and the other gods;
this is that supreme truth which the truth-speaking sage proclaimed.
The wise ones, such as the noble Avalokiteśvara and the noble Maitreya, as well as the sages, worship that through the yoga of non-worship. (290)

Therefore, because its nature is indivisible and because reality has been awakened to by it, the body of the Tathāgata is so designated, and not that of another, due to the latter's lack of such awakening. (291)
For one who practices this and dwells in non-apprehension, where could the mind become attached, or what could it hate, or even be deluded by? (292)
Whence could there be for him the arising of pain from the separation from the desired and so forth?
He is not smeared by worldly conditions, just as a lotus is not wetted by water. (293)
He has not departed from saṃsāra, yet he is free from the suffering of saṃsāra;
he has not attained nirvāṇa, yet he abides as if in nirvāṇa. ||294||
He is not afflicted by the heat of the fire of the afflictions, being like space even though possessed of afflictions;
he is neither without mind nor is he mindless, for he relies upon meditative attainments. ||295||
Having ascended the peak of the mountain of wisdom, Aśoka, out of the power of compassion, gazes upon the world that is tormented by grief and afflicted by suffering. (296)
Then, beholding the world with an eye moistened by compassion, he saw it enveloped in a web of conceptual constructions produced by the craft of discursive thought. (297)
Afflicted by the wounds of the arrows of birth, death, old age, disease, and sorrow;
wretched, miserable, unwell, protectorless, and without refuge. ||298||
Falling into a great flood of suffering, with a deluded mind, one who has set out with the desire for the cessation of suffering instead acts to increase the causes of suffering. (299)
In Śiva, who is the cessation of phenomenal expansion, as pure as the autumnal sky, the nectar of reality is beyond the range of the eye whose mental activity is devoid of light. (300)
Though being tormented, he was consecrated by compassion to bestow benefit upon them; he was a virtuous one, the supreme among beings, possessing the great essence of a diamond-like mountain. (301)

One who is devoted to generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, acting according to the time and according to one's capacity, with wisdom and mindfulness as the forerunners. ||302||
Originating from the mountain of generosity and the other perfections, these auspicious rivers with the pure waters of merit flow forth solely for the benefit of all sentient beings. (303)
To all supplicants at all times, by means of all external and internal objects, he dispels the suffering of poverty and the pain of begging. ||304||
Fulfilling the hopes of those in need and delightful at every moment, he who always yields inexhaustible fruit is a fortunate man who acts like the wish-fulfilling tree. (305)
His birth occurs only among the Sugatas for the sake of arising in the welfare and happiness of others;
or, by his own will, it may occur elsewhere for the same purpose of arising in the welfare and happiness of others. (306)
With a retinue consisting of devoted and pure attendants, in every rebirth he is filled with floods of merit through many gateways, like the ocean. //307//
With a mind that is skillful and undistracted through the realization of what is to be known, and joined with innate intelligence, one may remain for as many eons as desired. ||308||
And through the attainment of samādhi, which is incalculable and immeasurable, there is the wise state of mind and the adornment of infinite world-systems with ornaments. (309)
The manifestation of the ripening of karma through the performance of artistic and manual crafts, and taking birth according to one's wish, out of a desire to act for the benefit of the world. (310)
The vision of world-systems completely filled with the forms of Buddhas, and the manifestation of Buddha-fields at any desired time for the sake of awakening. ||311||
The vision of all knowable reality with the eye of wisdom, the knowledge of the established order of phenomena, and the attainment of mastery over names and so forth. (312)
The simultaneous or sequential shaking of infinite worlds through the expansion of supernatural power, as well as the blazing and raining from the body; 313.
The manifestation of all infinite directions by her own radiance, and the display of the hells and other realms for the sake of instilling urgency in the gods and others; (314)
And the sight of the Buddhas, the kinsmen of the world, together with their assemblies, who blaze with the light of immeasurable, wonderful, and inconceivable jewels of qualities. (315)
Desiring gold, gems, beryl, pearls, diamonds, and sapphires from the great mountains, he brings about even coolness for the fire. (316)
With a magnificent body that is unimpeded even by diamonds and other such obstacles, he performs wondrous coming and going in all directions in an instant. (317)
In the vision of entering into one's own body or even a single atom, and likewise [entering] infinite world-systems without causing suffering to sentient beings; ||318||
Desiring to contract or expand world-systems equal in number to the atoms [of the universe], or even of the same measure as a single atom, he acts [thus] above and below as well. (319)
Accompanied by the perfection of his stature, radiance, complexion, voice, and deportment,
he approaches the assemblies of Brahmā and others with the desire to discipline those who are to be trained. (320)
There, his appearance and disappearance are unknown to anyone;
impelled by compassion, he even effects the subjugation of others. //321//
By his will, he establishes the world under his control in its movements, stations, and utterances;
he bestows the joy of eloquence upon those who are devoid of it. (322)
He emits rays of light for the sake of pacifying those tormented by suffering in hell, and he also causes them to come into the assemblies of the lords of gods and others. (323)
Filling the directions with emanations according to those to be trained, he produces extraordinary joy through rains of the jewels of his teachings. ||324||
The state of having a body immeasurable across the three times, the perfection of the Buddha-field, and the dissolution and evolution of immeasurable world-systems; ||325||
One visualizes the field of the Sugatas within one's own body, or that very body within oneself;
and by will, one stabilizes the body of the Sugata within one's own field. ||326||
Having caused [the light] to emerge from his rays, from the pores of his skin, from his four [teeth], from the atmosphere,
and from his emanations, it became a festival for the ears.
Filling the worlds with a voice that was pervasive and boundless, clear and as charming as the call of the kalaviṅka bird, and deep, noble, and resonant.

According to the power of their inclinations and faculties, he teaches the Dharma in many ways for the sake of disciplining those to be trained—a Dharma that is auspicious and has tranquility as its sole flavor. (329)
It is afflicted, accompanied by latent tendencies, or pure; associated with pleasure, pain, and so forth;
inferior, intermediate, or sublime; and characterized by right resolve and the like. ||330||
Whatever kind of mind beings possess, wherever it may be, and for however long it lasts—even if they are many—he knows that very thing in its suchness, in that place, and for that duration. (331)
With his divine eye, he sees all forms everywhere—those that are divinely created and subtle, as well as those that possess the opposite qualities. (332)
With divine hearing, he hears divine and noble sounds produced by wealth, as well as human sounds—whether they are distant, contrary, or otherwise. (333)
He remembers his own former births everywhere, as well as those of all sentient beings; he causes others to remember them too, according to the distinctions of name, clan, and so forth. (334)

He knows the embodied beings everywhere—those established in the fruits of various desired and undesired actions across the different realms of existence, as well as those passing away, having passed away, and those newly born. (335)
In immeasurable world-systems, he disciplines those to be trained by manifesting the descent from Tuṣita, the entry into the womb, the attainment of perfect enlightenment, and so forth. (336)
Desiring [to manifest] in as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in infinite world-systems, he remains unmoving from his own field even while being present in all those fields.
Having created by his own will as many bodies as he desires, and in each body as many hands, heads, and tongues, with each one likewise being of that same number; (338)
With variegated baskets of perfumes and flowers, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, as large as Mount Meru, and filled with the most excellent, abundant, and radiant fragrances; (339)
Moist with devotion, he offers worship to the perfectly awakened ones who are fully enlightened and intent on the welfare of the world; and he praises them repeatedly with hymns of praise. (340)
With immeasurable jeweled parasols and canopies adorned with nets of pearls, and bristling with the sprouts of shimmering jewel-rays; ||341||
With pillars radiant with beautiful balconies and draped with pearl necklaces, and adorned with variegated craftsmanship fashioned from a multitude of diverse and noble gems; ||342||
With gabled chambers blazing with hundreds of lamps whose light was the radiance of flaming jewels, and reaching toward the clouds, they made the directions variegated with their own splendor. (343)
That accomplished one repeatedly hears from them teachings through many methods, and he speaks them to others with words and syllables neither deficient nor excessive. (344)
Having reached the further shore of the perfections, this Supreme Person stands exalted by the accumulation of merit and wisdom throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons. (345)

Having become the sun of the Perfectly Awakened One, he awakens the pond of the lotuses of the intellects of those capable of liberation by means of the stainless rays of his speech, which remove all impurities.
With the waters of her speech, which are cooler than frost, necklaces of pearls, the moon, and sandalwood paste, she extinguishes the heat of the fire of mental affliction in embodied beings. 347.

It swiftly delivers people from the ocean of existence—with its whirlpools of birth, its surging waves of suffering, and its crocodiles of death—by means of the great rafts of the three vehicles. (348)
With floods of jewels of his own well-spoken words, which utterly quench the thirst [of the world],
he destroys the poverty of virtue that has existed in the world since beginningless time. (349)
