They lead the person—who is wandering through the wilderness of existence and lacks a guide for the Dharma—toward Nirvana once their eyes have been opened by wisdom. (350)

He treats the world, which has been bitten by the venomous snakes of affliction and has fainted while clinging to its own welfare, by means of the medicines of knowledge and wisdom as they truly are. (351)
Out of compassion, he awakens through the sounds of the drum of his teaching those helpless beings who have long lain dormant in ignorance within cyclic existence. (352)
For those bound by the shackles of craving within the long prison of saṃsāra, he effects their release from bondage through the defeat of the four Māras. //353//
Like a sacrificial fire that is never satiated with divine and human sense-objects,
it brings satisfaction to embodied beings through the auspicious nectar-essence of wisdom.
It roars the great lion’s roar of emptiness amidst the assemblies, removing the pride and intoxication of the knowledge of the wild elephants that are the non-Buddhist teachers. //355//
Surrounded by a halo with the splendor of the sky resembling Indra’s bow,
he possessed the beauty of the full and radiant marks and minor characteristics inherent in his station.
With a form that was peerless, surpassing all beauty, captivating to the mind and eye, and serving as an ornament for Lakṣmī herself; ||357||
And with speech endowed with miracles and possessing sixty aspects, he wins over the minds of gods, asuras, humans, and others. (358)
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, Viśveśa assumes all forms through both his body and his speech, according to the needs of those to be trained. (359)
Thus, the wise one who has taken refuge in this state attains a majesty that is the source of countless, immeasurable, and wonderful qualities. (360)

The third chapter, titled "The Quest for Knowledge of Reality," [ends with: By him who is encircled by a halo like the appearance of the sky, and who possesses the splendor of the primary and secondary marks, fully radiant and complete, abiding in his place. (356)
With a form that was peerless, surpassing all beauty, captivating to the mind and the eye, and serving as an ornament for Lakṣmī herself. ||357||
And with speech endowed with miracles and possessing sixty aspects, he wins over the minds of gods, asuras, humans, and others. (358)
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, through both his body and his speech,
Viśveśa assumes a universal form for the sake of those to be trained.
Thus, by relying upon this very step, the wise man attains a majesty that is a mine of countless, immeasurable, and marvelous qualities. (360)
The fourth chapter, titled "The Quest for Knowledge of Reality," which is the introduction to the ascertainment of the reality of the Śrāvakas.
Those of weak faculties and inferior inclinations, agitated by groundless fear, speak thus regarding this profound doctrine which is difficult to fathom. (1)
It is said that the body of the Teacher, whose intellect is non-conceptual, is not a [true] substratum;
for, being a body, it is not accepted as such, just like the body of a cowherd. (2)

The great awakening of the perfectly awakened ones is realized through the path beginning with right view that has been realized, because it is an awakening, just like the awakening of a disciple. //3//

The Teacher’s attainment of omniscient knowledge results from the excellence of his faculties; just as, despite there being no difference in the path, certain individuals possess the analytical insights (pratisaṃvid) as they desire. (4)
By this very same path, the exhaustion of the cognitive obscurations is to be understood;
for when there is consciousness, the activity [of cognition] is held to be like the obscuration of the afflictions. (5)
This path is also [required] in the Mahāyāna for the Sage to attain omniscience; because it belongs to a different vehicle, it is accepted just as it is in the Pratyekabuddhayāna. (6)
The Mahāyāna is not the word of the Buddha, because it is not included among the Sūtras and so forth, or because it teaches a different path, just like the Vedānta system. (7)
Or, because it denies both fruit and cause—just like the nihilistic view—it is not certain [as a Buddhist school], since it is not included within the eighteen Nikāyas. (8)
Cognition having form and so forth as its object exists even as something self-cognized;
for this reason, even the sublation by perception arises against the proponent of universals.
If it is argued that because of the qualification "in reality there is no birth of entities," no sublation by perception or [scriptural] cognition is possible; ||10||
"Though she is unapproachable in the ultimate sense, she is approachable because she is a woman, just like any other"—even such a statement would be faultless, though its content is flawed. (11)
If the vision of truth were not reality itself, it would follow that there is an absence of reality;
nor is that which resembles the gods of the Yona people accepted as reality. (12)

The existence of external sense-bases is indeed cognized because of the arising of a cognition bearing their appearance; just as the existence of one's own mind is accepted by you as a matter of preference. (13)
Moreover, if the existence of the mind is not accepted, then for you the world is not "mind-only.
And when the world is taken as the subject of the thesis, you have neither a logical reason nor an example. (14)
In this regard, it is maintained that what the opponent taught—being unable to endure the calamity to his own system according to the principle previously stated—is not tenable. (15)
The non-conceptual cognition of the Teacher is considered to have selflessness as its object, just as the intellect has the selflessness of the person as its domain. ||16||
His proof is sublated by a contradictory non-erroneous [reason], since the arising of cognitions such as those produced by application and so forth is denied. (17)

Since the object of knowledge is not established in any way whatsoever, that non-arising of the intellect with respect to it is what is to be understood as "perfect awakening," because there is no misconception regarding the reality of the object of knowledge. (18)

If it is argued that this cognition is intended to be devoid of conceptual construction regarding intrinsic nature and so forth, and that its substratum is thereby negated, then you are merely proving what is already established. (19)
And having superposed conceptual construction, there is the teaching of its being peaceful and so forth;
and when one practices the path consisting of right view and the rest, [the fruit arises]. (20)
Non-perception, lack of volition, silence, non-expression,
inaction, non-subsistence, lack of undertaking, and non-forgetfulness.
Likewise, stability [is established]. ||21||
Therefore, we maintain that the enlightenment of a Buddha is attained by this very path;
hence, there is no fault of proving what is already established, or else let the cultivation [of the path] itself be examined. (22)
That which is not contradicted by scripture and follows from inference—that is the reality; and for the wise, the cultivation of that very [reality] is likewise intended. (23)
That which is Buddha is not that other Buddha [who taught] the "Mother's Sweetmeat" (mātṛmodaka);
even here, this is the definitive conclusion that the Mahāyāna is not the word of the Buddha. ||24||

Furthermore, this path previously described is not capable of attaining the enlightenment of a Buddha, because it consists of awakening through the aspects of suffering and so forth, like the path of a Pratyekabuddha. ||25||
In this way, there arises a sublation of the opponent's position by means of inference; or else, there is the impossibility of an example, as well as the refutation of its occurrence therein. (26)
The knowledge of non-arising and the knowledge of exhaustion are not in accordance with reality from the perspective of ultimate truth;
because they involve conceptual construction like an illusion, for whom could there be a realization of them in reality? (27)
The argument concerning the existence of other vehicles has already been answered by this very [point].
Furthermore, how could an Arhat, given the continued existence of obscurations, deserve final nirvana? (28)

If it is argued that liberation is considered to be like that of a Buddha due to the abandonment of afflicted ignorance, that is incorrect, because of the non-existence of such [afflicted ignorance] in the case of the primary Buddha and the emanation Buddhas. (29)
In reality, there is no path within the Mahāyāna for the sake of the enlightenment of a perfect Buddha, because it possesses conceptualization and signs, just like the mundane path. (30)
Now, it might be argued: "If this path were unreal, then the destruction of the afflictions would also be non-existent;
because of its unreality, just as there is no destruction [of afflictions] due to the cognition of a man in a pillar. (31)
Just as for someone terrified by the delusion that there is a snake in a rope, the knowledge that the rope is merely entangled with a creeper arises as its antidote. (32)
Because the reason is fallacious, there is the abandonment of the debate by the proponent;
by this, the fact that it is the antidote to affliction has been answered. (33)
And our Mahāyāna is indeed Buddhist because it reveals selflessness and so forth, and because it proclaims the majesty of the Three Jewels, unlike the Disciple Vehicle (Śrāvakayāna). //34//
Due to sublation by counter-reasoning, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*), because the truths and so forth taught in the Mahāyāna are included within the Vinaya and other scriptures. (35)
Since the path for the attainment of omniscience is said in the Mahāyāna to be preceded by right view, for that reason [the opponent's] argument is unestablished. (36)
Because of the teaching on the arising and cessation of suffering, it is not held that suffering is unarisen;
since arisen suffering is empty of intrinsic nature, why is it not so perceived? (37)
Since it is conditioned, like an illusion; or since the aggregates are without outflows, do you consider the cognition of the truth of suffering to be right view? (38)
Painful sensation is suffering; how is there the state of suffering for birth and so forth?
Its destruction is also suffering, as is the state of suffering regarding the cause and the path. (39)
If suffering were [defined] by way of its being a cause, then suffering itself would be the origin;
and since suffering is merely figurative, how could the knowledge of that [origin] be the cognition of suffering? (40)

Knowledge whose object is suffering is not accepted as true in reality, because it is a cognition of suffering [only] from that perspective, just like the cognition of pain arising from being pierced by a thorn or similar causes. (41)

It is not logical for [the self] to be of the nature of origination because it is the cause of suffering, just as the blow of a sword and so forth [are not the self], or because it is mental, like the path. (42)

A cognition whose object is the cause of suffering is not considered a true [cognition] because it perceives [the cause] through aspects such as suffering itself; just like any other cognition that takes the cause of suffering as its object. (43)
There is no cessation for that which is unborn, because its prior existence has been refuted;
since arising is negated, it is not logical for the unborn to have cessation, just as in the case of a sky-flower. (44)
If cessation occurs when that which has not yet been born is being born, then cessation itself would be something already ceased;
O wise one, tell me otherwise according to the truth. (45)
Even cessation that has not arisen is not, from the perspective of ultimate truth, a cessation,
because it is an unarisen cessation, like non-analytical cessation. ||46||
Since cessation itself is impossible, what path can you seek?
And how can a path that is unarisen bring anything to him? (47)
The path is not for the sake of attaining liberation, because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), like anything else;
or because it has cessation as its object (*ālambana*), like any other cognition of cessation. (48)
Alternatively, because it has a general object as its focal point, or else because it is conditioned, the vision of suffering and so forth should be considered false, just like false cognition. (49)
By this [same reasoning], since right intention, exertion, and so forth are false, it does not follow for you that the truth of the path is true from the perspective of ultimate reality. (50)
Thus, through cultivation, one becomes so disciplined that one does not perceive suffering and the rest, because the object of perception always exists in such a way, in an invisible form. //51//
Furthermore, it might occur to someone of corrupted intellect— like a child—
that even liberation is not desired by you [Buddhists] because you do not perceive the truth. (52)
When suffering and its sufferer do not arise, who desires liberation for what?
Liberation is produced by illusion; it is said to be so because of the penetration of delusion. (53)

Since liberation from suffering and the like is held to result from the non-perception [of objects] in every respect, there is an impossibility of an illustrative example; therefore, the reason is likewise unestablished. ||54||
Since this very path, preceded by right view, is also taught in the Mahāyāna, for that reason [the opponent's argument] lacks proof. (55)
And indeed, whatever is well-spoken in the Vedānta, all that was spoken by the Buddha.
Therefore, there is a deficiency of examples; otherwise, let that which is doubtful be examined. ||56||

For those who dwell in the range of wisdom that is free from the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, whose view could there be, and from where could there be an activity that denies cause and effect? (57)
Just as the connection between cause and effect is recognized in the world, so too is that [connection] not denied; therefore, the reason is not unestablished (asiddha). //58//
The conventional object, graspable by the intellect of the ignorant, is within the range of direct perception;
because it is established here as before, even its sublation does not constitute a refutation [of the ultimate]. (59)

For when one deliberates upon the reasoning of the learned, perception does not contradict [the conclusion], just as in the case of one who asserts that "all phenomena are selfless and momentary. (60)

The reality of form does not become an object for the foolish, due to their lack of refinement in inner science, just as [the reality of] the emptiness of the self and so forth [is not an object for them]. (61)

The intellect of the foolish is not fit for the ultimate reality regarding the true nature of form, because it is blinded by the cataract of ignorance, just as [an intellect] cannot have nirvāṇa as its object. //62//
For, by the qualification that "in reality there is no birth of entities," neither perception nor [scriptural] cognition can serve as a sublation anywhere. (63)

Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality, all phenomena are peaceful and like space, femininity and so forth are not established; therefore, in the case of the example, for whom, and by what means, could sublation be considered? (64)

If, out of a desire to find fault, you claim that just as the woman to be approached, the act of approaching her, and the one who approaches exist as a triad, so too must the approach to a forbidden woman be established; 65.
If this is true, then there is indeed sublation by common experience; however, the qualification [“by one who knows the truth”] is unestablished.
Therefore, this counter-example is not capable of subverting our positive argument.
The wise know reality to be free from conceptual proliferation, self-cognizable, devoid of the impurity of discursive thought, liberated from multiplicity and unity, and tranquil. (67)
Therefore, it is not logical for the [Vedic] truth to be taught by a god such as the Yavanas, since they declare that God has his origin from deities such as Brahmā. (68)
The existence of the sense-bases, such as form and so forth, is accepted as an object of cognition;
that their existence is established in a general sense is precisely what we also accept. (69)

If it is argued that the existence of the sense-bases such as form is established as having the nature of being composed of the elements and so forth, then there is no supporting example, and there is a subverting counter-argument. (70)

The sense-bases (āyatanas) such as form are not accepted as being characterized by the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika), because they are the causes for the arising of cognitions that manifest themselves, just like the mind (manas). //71//

For the nature of mind and mental factors is well-established among those who possess mind and mental states; therefore, neither the reason nor the example is lost, nor is the thesis of the yogins destroyed. (72)
In the statement "this is representation-only," there is the negation of external objects;
since this is the meaning of the sentence, how can there be a loss of the thesis by abandoning that [negation]? (73)
No one of tranquil intellect is made by mere words;
there, the wise will discern the essence and the worthlessness of speech. (74)
The fourth chapter, titled "Entering the Determination of the Reality of the Śrāvakas," and: "Excessive Reasoning is Also Subversive. (70)

The sense-bases (āyatanas) such as form are not accepted as having the nature of primary elements (bhūta) and derivative matter (bhautika), because they are the causes for the arising of cognitions that manifest their own forms, just like the mind (manas). ||71||

For the nature of mind and mental factors is well-established among those who possess mind and mental factors; therefore, neither the reason nor the example is lost, nor is the thesis of the yogins destroyed. (72)
In the statement "this is representation-only," the external object is negated;
since this is the meaning of the sentence, how can there be a loss of the thesis by abandoning that [external object], given that it truly exists? (73)
The Fifth Chapter: An Introduction to the Ascertainment of the Reality of Yogācāra.
Other wise ones, who take pride in their own tenets, declare:
For the descent into the nectar of reality has been well-taught by the Yogācāras. ||1||

Because of the existence of the non-existence of duality, and because of the non-existence of duality itself, the ultimate reality (paramārtha) is indeed considered the object of cognitions such as "existent" and so forth. (2)
The state of non-existence, selflessness, suchness, and abiding as it is; that which is to be grasped by non-conceptual cognition, and furthermore, the realization of that very [reality]. (3)
Relying upon perception, non-perception arises;
relying upon non-perception, non-perception arises. ||4||
Because of the non-perception of the imagined and because of the non-apprehension of the dependent, those who see reality perceive the perfected nature. ||5||
Because designation has a cause, because otherwise there would be the destruction of duality, and because affliction is perceived, the existence of the dependent nature is asserted. (6)
This is the method of the Perfection of Wisdom for the attainment of omniscience;
it does not, however, have as its ultimate aim the negation of arising, cessation, and so forth. (7)
To this it is replied: for us, every word of the Tathāgata is authoritative, because he is a reliable teacher; indeed, a noble person acts on the basis of such authoritative instruction. (8)
Another person may have a mind that is doubtful or mistaken regarding other scriptures;
therefore, in order to bring about their realization, one must seek a logical method. 9.
For the existence of the non-existence of duality is not tenable because of its contradictory nature;
just as the existence of the non-existence of a sky-flower is either [impossible], or else there can be no conceptualization of its existence. (10)
If it is argued that there is no difference [between them] because, in reality, the imagined does not exist,
that is no answer, for it applies equally to the distinction between the characterized (lakṣya) and the characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
If its being that [other thing] is intended to be its non-abandonment of its own nature, then,
since it does not abandon its own nature, it is for that very reason already that state. (12)
In this way, for those who see reality, knowledge would have non-existence as its object;
yet that [non-existence] is not the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), because it is a cause for the cognition of what is non-existent. (13)
If it is maintained that cognition having non-existence as its object is non-conceptual, then surely even the cognition of form would be existent and non-conceptual. (14)
And if this cognition of form were not real because it appears as an object of apprehension, then the logical reason would be fallacious and the thesis would be undermined. (15)
Furthermore, the enlightenment of the Teacher would either be conceptual or possess an objective referent;
even if it were non-conceptual, it could not be an intellect that takes intrinsic nature as its object. (16)
Nor is there a non-apprehension of form and so forth through the apprehension of mind-only;
for the thesis is contradicted by what has been accepted and by common perception. (17)
Nor is it logical that the cognition of form and so forth occurs without an object, just as the cognitions of form and so forth arise in a dream due to the emergence of such an appearance. (18)
Since dream-cognition and the like are held to have mental phenomena (dharma) as their object,
there is thus a deficiency in the example, and the very reality [of external objects] is thereby denied. (19)
If the appearance of an object were considered the objective support of the mind,
then setting aside that appearance of an object, what other nature of the mind could there be? (20)
The desired [simile] does not hold, because for him [the Yogācāra], there is the appearance of duality due to the arising of something resembling another;
for the momentary crystal produced therein has not arisen from that [original] material cause. (21)
Because it arises differently when that [object] has ceased, that cognition is considered to be erroneous.
Due to the non-difference of its capacity, there is no appearance of duality, just as in the case of the nature of the absence of an object. //22//

The appearance of both self and other is not accepted for the mind, because it does not conform to its cooperative causes, as in the case of a reflection; therefore, the appearance of duality is unreal. (23)
If it is argued that the appearance as two is accepted because of the non-existence of the distinction between the means of cognition and its result, [we reply:
since that is established even otherwise, the postulation of that [distinction] is not desired. ||24||

That by which an object of cognition is cognized—namely, by means of knowledge that, while being born, bears the appearance of the object—is considered the instrument of valid cognition (pramāṇa). ||25||
And because it is observed that [the obstruction] ceases when that [knowledge] arises, the cessation of that [obstruction] is considered the fruit;
for there is likewise the realization of that whose nature is inexpressible. (26)
If it is intended to prove that an external object has the same nature as consciousness,
then it is like the immediately preceding [moment of consciousness], by virtue of being an object of cognition. (27)
For each [of these reasons], there would indeed be such fallibility;
the statement in the sūtras that "there is mind-only" is for the purpose of negating an agent and an enjoyer. (28)
If it is established that consciousness is empty of imagined objects, then because of the existence of non-imagined objects, there would be no refutation of objects. (29)
There is no doubt regarding the non-existence of things as they are not conceptualized by the nature of dream-cognition;
nor is [the dream] accepted as being without a basis, because the illustrative example is unestablished. (30)
Now, it might be argued that the object of cognition must be either a single entity or a collection;
yet, when examined through reasoning, neither of these two is tenable. (31)
In that case, however, a single [atom] is not the object of the cognition of form, because it does not appear as such;
just as the form of the sense organ itself is not the object because it does not appear as that. (32)
Even a plurality [of atoms] is not considered to be the object of the mind, for form [composed of] atoms lacks substantiality, like a double moon. //33//
In that case, if it is being proved by the opponent that a form not composed of atoms is within the range of the mind, then indeed what is already established is being proved.
Thus, the reason consisting of an accumulated form is unestablished, because the cognition arises with the manifestation of that [form] through the assistance provided by other forms. (35)
Its status as an objective referent is accepted because it is the cause of a cognition appearing as that;
therefore, your thesis is refuted by inference, just like [the case of] passion. (36)

If it is argued that cognition is established as being without an object because it arises from its own seed—just like mental cognition (manodhī)—then, since it is non-conceptual, would it not follow for you that it actually possesses an object? (37)
Alternatively, there is no refutation of [the properties] such as being a cognition by means of an inference without a [real] object;
since a collection is not what is being asserted, its negation does not constitute a contradiction. (38)
Even if an external object does not exist, the two—the capacity and the form of the object—are mutually causal; how then can their cessation be maintained? (39)
Because it is noble and non-conceptual, non-conceptual wisdom is not to be abandoned;
since its production [is required], how could there be liberation from the non-impairment of its seed? (40)
When the dualistic perception arises, the appearance of the manifold world is produced;
that appearance of the manifold to it is its own arising from its own seed. (41)
Dissolution occurs through the offering of power (śakti) into that [Self], either into one's own self or from another source.
But surely, this has been described as the Self itself, being a synonym for consciousness (vijñāna). (42)
Having understood duality to be like an illusion—crushed, unpeaceful, and non-self—one realizes non-duality as the imperishable, real, immortal, supreme state. ||43||

Because of the absence of universals therein and because of the cessation of conceptual construction, there exists a non-difference from liberation by taking [the object] as the support of non-conceptual cognition. (44)

In order to establish that there is mind-only (cittamātra), one must either accept that mental factors (caitta) are not distinct from the mind, or else the state of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā) cannot be maintained. ||45||

Or let it be accepted that the designation "mind" applies to the collection of feeling and the other aggregates; in that case, there would be a denial of atoms and an abandonment of one's own tenet system. (46)

If it is maintained that the mind is a substantial reality because of its defilement and purification, there is no contradiction, since that is established by the fact that feelings and so forth arise in such a manner. ||47||

Just as the continuity of leaves and so forth arises from the manifold potencies of the lotus root, so too do the diverse functions of the mental continuum arise from the mind, which exists as a non-substantial reality.
Non-arising results from the counteragent; arising occurs when a cause is present.
Since it lacks substantial reality, the conceptualization of a variegated arising and so forth is not accepted here. //49//
There is no liberation by taking that as an object, nor is there the cessation of the intellect;
therefore, whether from the perspective of conventional reality or ultimate truth, there is no equality with one who knows the self. (50)

Because it is unarisen even by way of intrinsic nature, because it is not a substantial entity, and because it is subject to destruction, it is empty of form and so forth like an illusion; through such practice, one becomes free from attachment. //51//

Moreover, even though form and the other [aggregates] exist, through the realization of them as they truly are, the grasping at what is non-existent is indeed turned away; when they do not exist, why would that [grasping] not occur then? (52)
Furthermore, the conceptualization of substantial entities is the domain of the mind and mental factors;
even when form and the other [objects] have been negated, it ought not to proceed. (53)
If, in order to refute those [objections], you accept another injunction, then remember:
"It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. (54)
A conceptualization [of the world] as being like a snake is not desired, because it is a mental construction;
for since the rope-nature is not invariably [the case], even perception serves as a sublater.
Because that [cognition] perceives a portion of that [object], it is not an error, since it possesses multiple aspects;
furthermore, for you, there would be a denial of the reality of things due to the total negation of the object. (56)
Even in the absence of that [external object], defilement does not arise from the activity of names toward objects.
Because afflictions are observed even in animals that have direct perception of verbal expressions. ||57||
Furthermore, since the cognition of form arises in dependence upon the verbal expression "form," it is not tenable to conceive that form is empty of its own intrinsic nature. (58)
The object of cognition is that which appears as a thing excluded from what is non-material in nature;
that is the self-nature of matter. Therefore, the emptiness of matter is untenable because of its existence. //59//
For a universal is indeed expressible, yet no universal exists at all;
thus, it is not tenable that it is empty of an expressible nature.

The object possessing a universal is that which is to be expressed, because it is the cause of a cognition appearing as that [universal]. Since it exists by way of that very nature, its ineffability is not tenable. (61)
Emptiness of what is heterogeneous [is established] because it is the cause for the occurrence of a uniform cognition;
it is determined that the universal is the universal among those of the same class. (62)

If the substratum is not apprehended, the object of cognition cannot be apprehended, just as [the number] cannot be; since it is apprehended when that [substratum] is apprehended, the entity to be postulated must likewise be so, and thus it should not be desired as something separate. ||63||
Because it is non-different [from the universal], exists [in all individuals], and is a substance, it resides in many [individuals] as one;
and because it does not perish when that [individual] perishes, there is no cognition of it in another [individual]. Nor is there [such a cognition] in what is not that [universal]. (64)
There is no separation [between them] because their forms are non-distinct as "non-blue" and "non-lotus";
for grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) arises from the two terms functioning with respect to a single object. //65//
The exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is not a universal distinct from other properties, just like a particular;
nor can there be a difference in cognition regarding things such as blankets and the like, because non-existence is devoid of differentiation.
Since this [universal] is not apprehended when the object is not apprehended, its status as being conceptualized or denotable is not accepted;
if it were denotable by means of that [object], then its own status as being denotable and so forth would be lost. (67)
According to the Yogācāra system, it is not at all logical to maintain that a real entity, whose nature is distinct from anything else, is inexpressible, even when associated with the mind. (68)
Because things are empty of the nature of verbal expression, they lack intrinsic nature;
and for that very reason, because they are unarisen, they are neither produced nor ceased. (69)
Since an entity possessing verbal expression is not described in the same way as it appears, it has been extensively stated that "phenomena lack substantial reality," and so forth. (70)
If it is stated that the dependent nature exists conventionally, you are proving what is already established.
If it is stated that it exists in reality, there is no corroborative example, and the reason is also contradictory. (71)
If the lack of intrinsic nature in arising is due to the non-arising of what is already existent, then it is not a valid support for the negation of non-arising, cessation, and so forth. (72)
The Sage declared that whatever is born from conditions is unborn, because its production by way of intrinsic nature is negated from the perspective of ultimate reality. (73)

And because phenomena are unreal, the varied operations of cognition and language regarding their specific and general characteristics are not contradicted from the perspective of conventional reality. (74)
For by whatever name each phenomenon is expressed, that phenomenon does not exist therein; such is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā). //75//

Now, if [it is argued that] an intrinsic nature produced from conditions is not intended [by us], and [you claim] its arising is due to dependence [on others], then [we reply]: it is like an illusion; there is no real existence. (76)
Furthermore, the non-apprehension of the dependent nature is held to result from its not being born by way of intrinsic nature;
for it is not logical that there should be a false appearance of that which has been born in the ultimate sense. //77//
Since they exist in the manner that they appear, by virtue of having that appearance as their nature, how could phenomena not be like an illusion, given that they exist exactly as they appear? (78)
Because it is not born through a truly existent self, there is the state of being unarisen and unceasing;
likewise, because it is a non-entity and lacks intrinsic nature, it is also devoid of substantial existence. (79)
Because designation is equivalent to mere-cognition (vijñaptimātra), it possesses no fault;
since neither that which is to be abandoned nor the abandoner exists, for whom could weariness and so forth be intended? (80)
Since liberation occurs through the cessation of conceptual construction even in the absence of substantiality,
it does not follow [that liberation is impossible] even when there is substantial existence, because [the self] is unproduced.
Such a postulation is not accepted. ||81||
If there were no real entity (*vastu*), even conventional designation (*prajñapti*) could not exist.
One who holds such a view is a nihilist (*nāstika*), unfit for conversation, and indeed one with whom it is impossible to dwell. (82)
"Being itself subject to ruin,
it causes others to suffer grief"—
this is the vomiting forth of the bait of hatred.
It indicates indigestion caused by pride. ||83||

Because they lack an intrinsic nature, because they are the cause of delusion for the foolish, and because they come into being after not having existed, phenomena are considered to be like an illusion. (84)

The equality with space is not appropriate for an object that is free from conceptual construction, because it provides the opportunity for the manifestation of various perceptions and conceptual constructions. //85//
Once [the object] has arisen, it cannot be inexpressible because of the refutation stated previously;
even if it were inexpressible, there would be a delusion regarding reality within conventional truth. (86)

If the vision of reality is desired because another reality exists within a reality, then why is the vision of reality not also desired in the case of a jar, since two jars do not exist within it? (87)

Neither for the purpose of concealing a flaw in policy, nor regarding the defilement and purification of those [elements], would they [the qualities] exist, because gold and the like conform to their conditions. (88)
Just as space appears as either defiled or pure depending on the purity or impurity of the eyes, yet space itself is eternally pure; so too is the true nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena. (89)
The delusion of cognition regarding its being afflicted and so forth is a property of the agent, not of the object;
purity does not have that as its objective support, for reality is not held to be an object of apprehension. (90)
If reality were a substantial entity, then—as before—there would be a confluence of faults;
furthermore, that cognition [of reality] is not considered to be supramundane and non-conceptual, because it would be subject to cessation. (91)
The intellect remains obscured by darkness as long as it conforms to the object of knowledge;
as long as cognition arises, there is conformity to the object of knowledge. (92)
Because it is impossible for knowledge to obscure itself—just as a sword-blade cannot cut itself—and because self-obscuration is negated, omniscience could not occur instantaneously. ||93||
As before, because birth is rejected, it is not yet born and lacks substantial existence;
it is apprehended by the non-conceptual wisdom of the noble ones and is in every way inexpressible. (94)
If even the existence of existence-and-non-existence were an ultimate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
how could there be for you liberation from the extremes of superimposition and denial? (95)
There is no existence in reality because there is no birth, and no non-existence because of the absence of that [existence].
Therefore, the reality intended is non-dual, being free from the duality of existence and non-existence. //96//
The Teacher would not be without an object of focus, because he takes suchness as his object;
nor is awakening simply equanimity, because there is a distinction between reality and its own manifestation. (97)
How could that cognition which has suchness as its object be one whose power is not implanted? It is not logical for a cognition to be like a sky-flower insofar as it lacks an implanted power. (98)
The reality of things has not been described as being either identical or different, due to the concealment of one's own method (*svanaya*).
Because it is neither a substance nor perceivable, our position is logical, exactly as it has been stated. (99)

Because it is without birth and thus devoid of distinctions, it is equal to space; because it is unstained, it is absolutely inexpressible, for it cannot be grasped by the intellect in any way whatsoever. //100//
The supramundane intellect is considered to be free from the cataract of arising;
it is so called either because it delivers one from the world or because it transcends the world. (101)

It is non-conceptual, without objective support, and signless; by means of that [wisdom], through the simultaneous awakening to the equality of non-awakening, it is realized as its own and others' true nature. (102)
The non-arising of phenomena is indeed called the selflessness of phenomena;
there, as before, there can be no occurrence of the stain of conceptual construction. (103)

If it is argued that because reality is not accessible through reasoning, its realization does not come from inference, and therefore the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not apprehended by means of logic; 104.
Here, through inference that is faultless and conforms to scripture, the entire flood of various imagined conceptual constructions is eliminated. (105)
The Buddhas, whose minds are like space regarding the true nature of all that is knowable, perceive through non-conceptual gnosis by way of non-seeing. (106)
Therefore, reality is not apprehended as the object of inference;
rather, by means of that [inference], there is the refutation of whatever is the opposite of the knowledge of reality. (107)

When cognitions have come to differ due to the differences between various scriptures, what other method capable of critical examination exists, even though the scripture itself remains the same? (108)
The refutation of an opposing position is not accepted as being established by mere assertion;
and as long as the opposing position has not been negated, how can there be non-conceptual cognition? (109)
Therefore, the Sage who perceives reality has taught the doctrine of the two truths, because the realization of the ultimate truth depends upon relying on conventional usage. (110)

Because it possesses an object, even though that object is suchness, it is false—just like the cognition of dreams and so forth; therefore, its being an object of apprehension is not logically tenable as reality. (111)
The Dharma has been described by the Lord of Sages as ungraspable, ineffable, and devoid of the movement of the intellect; yet, such being the case, that [Dharma] is contradicted.
Therefore, that reality which was previously illustrated as being endowed with both reasoning and scripture remains uncontradicted when examined by means of such reasoning. (113)
Some are ensnared by the tree of the aggregates;
some are bound by the net of consciousness.
Even on the vast expanse of ultimate reality,
the Victorious One has not fallen.
He sports within the heart-mind. //14//

The fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Reality of Yogācāra": Even because it has unreal suchness as its object, like the cognition of dreams and so forth, that which is grasped by it is not real; therefore, [its being] reality is not tenable. (111)
The Dharma has been described by the Lord of Sages as ungraspable, ineffable, and devoid of the movement of the intellect; yet, such being the case, that [Dharma] is contradicted.
Therefore, that reality which was previously illustrated as being endowed with both reason and scripture remains uncontradicted when examined by means of this very reasoning. (113)
