some...
The Sixth Chapter: An Introduction to the Principles of Sāṃkhya.
For Nature (prakṛti) is indeed insentient, composed of the three qualities (guṇas), and characterized by productivity.
The person who constantly practices [this] is the opposite of this [world]. ||1||

When that [object] exists as a real entity within the mind, it arises for the person either through the emergence of a reflection that conforms to the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), or else through [the person's own] transformation (*pariṇāma*). (2)
Through such vision of reality—that "I am one and Prakṛti is another"—the person whose activities and instruments have ceased is said to be liberated. ||3||
"Neither 'I' nor 'mine'—through the grace of the Fully Awakened One who has accomplished his purpose, primordial nature (prakṛti) is liberated"; thus the Sāṃkhyas proclaim the truth. (4)
In this regard, the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa have been explained according to their respective logical connections;
however, they must be examined further, for the Self is not held to be mere consciousness. (5)
Consciousness is the awakening to the objects of knowledge; in the absence of objects of knowledge, it does not exist.
What, then, could the self be now—conscious or unconscious? (6)
That which has not been burnt does not burn, according to logic, because of the absence of anything to be burnt, just as before;
therefore, the conscious self is not established by the analogy of burning. ||7||
For that which possesses the form of awakening is intended as the "awakening of the intellect" (buddhibodha);
since an entity must reside in a substance, and this [awakening] resides in the person (puruṣa). ||8||
In the unchanging Puruṣa, this rule regarding its own nature is inconsistent;
for there is no consciousness other than awareness—what else could be postulated? (9)
If it should be thought that consciousness is not identical with the intellect because it possesses a cause, just like a jar, and therefore consciousness is not the intellect; [then we reply: 10.
If you argue that the difference of cognition from consciousness is what is to be proven, this is not our view;
for if you claim that [consciousness] is absent in cognition, you contradict your own accepted tenet. (11)
Furthermore, consciousness in that which is unborn is not logical because of its state of being unborn.
If it were to exist despite being non-existent, then it would follow that consciousness itself is indeed that [unborn] entity. (12)

Since it is maintained that the cognition of the omniscient one is not distinct from the mental modification [of the object], there would have to be non-distinction even if a difference existed; yet since that difference does not exist, that [omniscience] is also non-existent. (13)
Now, it might be argued that even the cognition of a self is considered to be true in some cases, while in others it is the opposite, like the cognition of a post as a post [when it is not one]. (14)
If it is argued that [the self] is real in some respect according to conventional truth, then this is a proof of what is already established;
for we do not maintain that the object of the mind is real as a self. (15)

Furthermore, regarding the validity of cognition characterized by [attributes such as] omnipresence and so forth, there is no illustrative example whatsoever, either in reality or conventionally. (16)
There can be no emergence of consciousness in the insentient, nor any modification of the sentient;
for whom, then, could there be the arising of the knowledge of reality, by which liberation will be attained? (17)

Even if this [intellect] were favored by consciousness, the determination of "I" and so forth would be improper due to its lack of sentience; how much more so when that [consciousness] is absent? (18)
Nor is its cessation logical, because it is common to many;
as it is held that [the status] of a maidservant is like that of a woman who has had one lover and is now dead. (19)
How can there be a restriction on the vision of reality for a person whose mind has manifested existence, given that there is no obstruction due to the difference in location among other selves? (20)
And in the cognition of sound and so forth, dharma, adharma, and the like are likewise [unperceived];
since the objection applies equally, even an unperceived restriction does not exist. (21)
The person (puruṣa) is neither insentient, nor a cause, nor indeed all-pervading;
for if there were a transformation of the person, it would be like the transformation of curd. 22.
Because consciousness, though unchanging, serves as the cause for the reflection, it becomes associated with the aforementioned defects, just like the reflection of a face in a mirror. (23)
And because the person is devoid of conceptual construction, it is not tenable to say "I am other [than the body]";
if it is argued that there is no fault on account of metaphorical designation, then liberation would be merely metaphorical. (24)

Pradhāna exists because of the continuity among diverse things, because of transformation, because of the relationship between cause and effect, because of power, and because of the manifestation of manifold forms. ||25||
Whatever has been stated is like the parts of a pot and so forth;
and since differences likewise possess that [nature], therefore differences have a cause. ||26||
If it is being proved that particular differences have a cause, that is proving what is already established;
furthermore, because the positive concomitance is unestablished, the reason would be unestablished. (27)

If it is claimed that [the particular] is preceded by the universal because it possesses a universal, then there is no illustrative example, whether from a universal or a particular, as in the previous case. ||28||

It is not held that [the self] has pleasure and so forth as its intrinsic nature, like the aggregate of feeling; because it is an aggregate, [this would lead to] a deviation from the rule in each case, such as with pleasure, pain, and so on. (29)
Alternatively, because delusion is itself a form of feeling, the example would be deficient;
furthermore, since its existence is established by the fact that it possesses a cause, it is not [unestablished], just like suffering, pleasure, and so forth. (30)
Even if deviation is thus excluded, there remains the state of the self being unrefined, because the thesis is sublated by the inference based on positive concomitance and so forth. ||31||

Because [the reasons] such as "being unproduced" and "having infinite existence," along with their specific qualifications, have been refuted, and because they are observed even in the case of the qualities of Pradhāna, these reasons are inconclusive (vyabhicārin). //32//
If they were preceded by a single cause, there would be contradiction among them;
likewise, if they have distinct causes, no illustrative example exists.
It is understood that sandalwood is not destroyed at the moment a chip arises from it, because of the proximity of its power, form, measure, and so forth, just like the wood itself. (34)

Therefore, if [the opponent argues that] the reason is not unestablished because it is distinct [from the effect], then if its existence is asserted by way of its nature as a potency (*śakti*), there is no illustrative example, just as before. //35//
If its existence were asserted through a manifested form, there would be an abandonment of the established conclusion (kṛtānta);
for even in the proof [of causality], the identity of cause and effect is maintained according to the logic already stated. //36//
If the principle of "being born once" is used to prove oneness, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*).
Furthermore, if one posits other meanings for that term, there is a convergence of faults as before. (37)
By this, the inferential nature of previous cognitions is also refuted;
for their causes are always subject to deviation due to pleasure, pain, and so forth. (38)
Because there is no non-difference in reality... nor as stated before.
If there were non-difference despite the difference in time, there would be a contradiction with established usage and scripture. (39)
If it is argued that non-existence is not established when sandalwood is concealed,
that is refuted by the statement regarding [the perception of] time with its remaining parts, just as in the case of the present moment. (40)
Even so, one should not lack the resolve to guard the vulnerabilities in one's own policy;
for the fault of others does not attach itself [to us], just as a pot does not become wet when water is poured from it. (41)
If the meaning of the reason "because of having that nature" is taken as a conceptual alternative, there is the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra);
furthermore, if it refers to the state of non-difference, the reason would be unestablished (asiddha). ||42||

If it is maintained that the ear and other [senses] possess the status of an enjoyer because they are insentient, then if you mean "eating" by those whose specific nature is not specified, it is a case of proving what is already established. ||43||
Furthermore, how can there be attachment to such distinctions as being indifferent or eternal?
For even though consciousness exists, the state of being an enjoyer is not admitted because of its lack of activity. (44)
The inactivity of entities, however, is established by their being objects of cognition;
for whatever is stated in such a manner is perceived as such, like pleasure and delusion. (45)
Even suffering must be admitted as inactive, because it possesses a cause, or because it is insentient, or because it is expressible, or because it is cognizable, just like delusion. (46)

For one who desires that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and other [logical marks] be causes while maintaining their distinctness, it is true that there is no deviation from them by means of the qualities of primordial matter (*pradhāna*). (47)
The [existence of] cause, effect, and so forth is established through inference based on having a cause;
thus, for you, reasons accompanied by such qualifications would indeed be contradictory. (48)
The sixth chapter, titled "Entering the Reality of Sāṃkhya," ends here. Furthermore, it is accepted even when those [causes] exist. ||44||
The seventh chapter of the *Vaiśeṣikatattvāvatāra*: "The Inactivity of Entities," because they are objects of cognition.
The followers of Kaṇāda maintain that in liberation there is no cognition of the principles such as earth and so forth,
because their specific qualities have not been apprehended, just like the cognition of the principle of the individual soul and so forth.
"Even regarding the reality of the Vaiśeṣika, [this work] does not cause the cataracts of false views;
thus, because it is devoid of fallacious reasoning, it inspires joy in the intellect. (28)
The Seventh Chapter, titled "Introduction to the Principles of Vaiśeṣika.
The Eighth Chapter.
The Entrance into the Ascertainment of the Reality of Vedānta:

The proponents of Vedānta say that one who knows the Self is difficult to find outside [this tradition]. How can there be liberation for those who hate the Self, the proponents of the doctrine of empty mental impressions? (1)
Beyond darkness, having realized the Great Puruṣa, who possesses the splendor of the sun,
as the Maheśvara Ātman, the wise man transcends death.
When the seer beholds the golden-hued Maker, the Lord, then, having cast off both evil and merit, he shall attain supreme equanimity. ||3||
The past, the present, and the future are held to be the Puruṣa;
he is within and without, in the far distance and in the near, and he is the performer of action.
From that, all beings are born, like threads from a spider;
into that they dissolve, and the wise do not undergo rebirth again.
Immortality is not desired for a mortal, just as coldness is not desired for fire;
therefore, immortality is attributed to the immortal person due to the lack of awakening [to that state]. (6)
Since there is nothing higher than him, since there is no one greater than him, or even more minute than him—by him alone is this entire universe pervaded. (7)
That is subtle and gross, endowed with both,
the sovereign who exercises mastery over the primary principle.
Having reached the ultimate limit of desire,
the yogi proceeds according to his wish. //8//
For one who perceives thus, all beings become the Self alone;
there is equality among the ignorant and the learned, the outcaste and the brahmin, and so forth. 9.
Just as space does not possess the nature of a jar during its production or destruction,
so too the Self is not held to possess the nature of the body and such during their arising and passing away. (10)

If it is argued that, due to non-difference, the multiplicity of the one [Self] is like that of the space within jars, and its unity is like that which results from the difference between jars—such being the view held regarding the equality of all things; 11.
Just as there is no difference whatsoever in the clay even when there is a difference in pots and so forth, likewise, although bodies are distinct, [there is no difference in the nature].
I have no attachment whatsoever. //12//
Just as when a single pot-space is covered by dust, smoke, and so forth, that condition does not belong to all [spaces], because space is not of the nature of pleasure and the like. (13)
Due to lack of awakening, one who does not know the Self accumulates karma and experiences its fruit— whether auspicious or inauspicious— just like one who possesses deluded conceit in a dream.
Though residing in the body, he is not defiled while experiencing [objects], because of his non-attachment;
like a king who acts according to his will, he is not at fault for the evil [of worldly involvement]. //15//
When the yogi, practicing yoga, realizes that one supreme, all-pervading, eternal, and infallible state which is Brahman, he does not undergo rebirth again. ||16||
It is eternal and free from conceptual construction, that which is beyond the range of words; yet speech is employed there by those whose intellects are led astray by distinctions. (17)
In this matter as well, those who are free from partiality investigate;
for one whose mind is shrouded by attachment to a particular side does not perceive the truth, even though it exists. (18)
The existence of a self and likewise its status as the cause of the world have been refuted;
therefore, liberation resulting from the vision of such [a self] is merely a conceptual construction. (19)
The innate view of a self-identity exists even in animals and leads to their lack of peace;
since it is the root of all afflictions, you have indeed caused it to increase. (20)
For those possessed by the view of a self-identity and engrossed in the notions of "mine" and "I," saṃsāra is cultivated; from that very source, liberation is also said to arise. (21)

If peace were to arise from seeing that [self], it would be like the cessation of intoxication through further intoxication; it would be like the recovery of one suffering from a triple-humor disorder (saṃnipāta) due to indigestion through eating more food. ||22||
The proponents of the Vedas assert that this self is of two kinds.
The self bound within the body is called "the fettered," while the self abiding in the supreme state is "the liberated. //23//

Just as the cognition that "the self is real" is not directed toward others or the self [as it appears], so too the cognition of a self with respect to the body and so forth arises from such a reflective awareness regarding the self itself. (24)
Even if a person were merely imagined, what could he do for you?
If you say it is the cognition of objects such as form and sound, that is not tenable. (25)
Cognitions regarding objects such as form arise [from conditions] and do not have the self as their agent, because their birth is dependent upon causal conditions, like fire from a sun-crystal. (26)
And that sound which consists of phonemes is also held not to have itself as its agent,
because it is audible or because it is sound, just like an echo. (27)
By this, the remaining actions—such as going and coming, characterized by the movement of the hands, feet, and so forth, which arise from the body—are refuted. (28)
Through the exclusion [of others], there is the perception of a name; the recollection of memory;
the discernment through a mode, which is the understanding of wisdom; and the cognition of knowledge. (29)
Nor is any other effect of the self perceived, nor is its intrinsic nature determined; like a sky-flower, even its existence is not determined. (30)

If it is argued that the status of being an instrument is established for knowledge and so forth because they are called instruments, or if their being caused by another agent is established—like the giver—that is not logical. (31)
Since these [terms] arise as suffixes in the active sense (kartari), they do not possess the status of an instrument (karaṇa);
therefore, the reason is either unestablished (asiddha) or inconclusive (anaikāntika). ||32||
For knowledge and the other [faculties] possess agency because they are designated by the word "agent";
just as in the observed case, "Devadatta cuts," agency is attributed here [to them]. (33)
In a collection of conditioned phenomena that is itself devoid of activity, the designation of "agent" would apply by virtue of its being an instrument, just as you say, "the lamp illuminates. (34)
In reality, there is no primary agent, for indeed there is not even a single maker of a jar;
therefore, metaphorical agency is not admitted in the case of lamps and the like.
The mind, under the sway of passion and the like, is attached to the sphere of form and other objects; it is bound and unable to attain liberation, imprisoned within the prison of saṃsāra. (36)
This collection of hands and so forth,
which possesses consciousness and is designated as a "sentient being," is called a "donor" and so on due to the arising of volition such as renunciation. (37)
Upon the arising of knowledge, through the cessation of the fetters such as ignorance, one who is liberated from the bonds of passion and so forth is designated as "liberated. (38)
But in a self that is like space, all this is very difficult to maintain;
or let your self be a flower in the sky, if the self is exceedingly dear to you. (39)
For if the self is held to be of the nature of cognition by its very essence, then its unity is not tenable, because it would depend upon instruments and other such factors. (40)
Or, if there exists an object of knowledge such as a self, that cognition does not cease;
for even a lamp that has fulfilled its purpose is seen to continue arising from its own causes. (41)
As long as the arising of knowledge exists for one who is mindful, so long is the seed accumulated;
just as long as there is the production of an echo, so long does the echo persist. ||42||
And how can there be saṃsāra for one who knows, and how can there be knowledge without an instrument?
Since [the Self] is always distinct [from these], from what and how could bondage and liberation arise? (43)
For one who maintains the doctrine of a single self, there can be no liberation even through suffering, nor is there liberation in liberation itself;
because the self is non-different from that [suffering], just as fire is non-different from its heat. (44)
And how could one whose intellect is dissolved or unarisen be a knower without an instrument?
For just as Pūrṇaka is not fit to be a cutter without an axe. (45)
Just as when it is said, "He burns with fire," it is the fire that burns and not the agent;
likewise, when it is said, "He knows by means of the intellect," it is knowledge that knows, and not the person for you [the Sāṃkhyas]. (46)
Its establishment is not like that of a potter, because it does not possess that nature;
nor is its establishment desired to be like that of fire, since fire cannot exist in the absence of combustible matter. (47)

And how could that which is ignorant become the knower, the agent, and the enjoyer according to you? Being like space and free from conceptual construction, it can only be conceived through scripture alone. (48)
Furthermore, that which is neither ignorant nor wise could not possess either an intrinsic nature or a lack of intrinsic nature;
and that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot be a self, just like the son of a barren woman. (49)
For one whose suffering or favor arises from the suffering or favor of another, that [other] is not truly his self, just as the sky is not Devaśarman’s. ||50||

If meditation, knowledge, and so forth are desired for the liberation of a self that is distinct from [the body], then effort would be directed toward what is not the self; how then could a mortal become immortal? (51)
If the inner self were different from the [individual] self, ...
[your] proposition would be abandoned. ||52||
If the inner self were not distinct from the self, then your proposition would be abandoned. ||53||
If it is subtle, it is not large; if it is large, it does not possess subtlety.
Furthermore, it is not a single material phenomenon; how then could it exist within a self that is immaterial? (54)

It is not logical that a single entity should possess multiple natures based on the example of the elephant, because the trunk is not accepted as being the elephant itself, nor is there unity among the trunk and its other parts. (55)
If the self were to possess the color of the sun and so forth, how could it be colorless? Moreover,
based on the analogy of the *palāśa* leaf, a multiplicity of forms for the self is not desired.
For there is no single palāśa tree that is always of a modified nature;
since its roots and other parts are not one, they too are differentiated by their respective conditions. (57)
Seniority and superiority are held to be relative to something else;
how can their existence and the injunction [regarding them] be maintained if there is oneness? (58)
If the self were a substance, it would not be omnipresent because of its substantial nature; nor would it be eternal like a jar. Therefore, how could the world be filled by it? (59)
The status of being a substratum is appropriate for a substance, yet it is not appropriate for the self;
since it is unarisen like a flower in the sky, it therefore lacks the nature of a substratum. (60)
For one who perceives that all beings are indeed the Self alone, how could there be a non-Self for the Self? Just as it is not possible for an existing entity to lack existence. (61)
Therefore, there is no distinction [of the self] from the ignorant and others;
thus, it is without support and without illustration.
If the self were a single unity, the occurrence of a multitude of afflictions would be impossible.
Let it be observed that the self of Maitra is also [the self] of Caitra, because its form is non-different from Caitra’s, or else because there is no difference in location. (63)
He is the enjoyer of pleasure and pain; therefore, upon their liberation, he too must be liberated;
upon their bondage, he too is bound;
or rather, when they suffer, let him be the one who suffers. (64)
It is not the case that [the unity of the self] is impossible for all [beings] on the basis of the analogy of the space within a jar;
for even by you, the unity of space is not established. //65//
That which is the state of the absence of any substance is indeed conventional space;
therein is the movement of those who move,
and it is the room for those who require room.
Space is neither that which is unobstructed nor the giver of space;
if these were stated as its causes for its existence, the reason would be unestablished (asiddha). //67//
Nor is space accepted as an entity because it lacks a cause;
for that very reason, it is not even one, like the son of a barren woman. (68)
Clay, in its form as a jar and so forth, possesses unity through its belonging to the same genus of clay;
yet in other cases, such as a water-pot (kuṇḍa) and the like, it is different and different—therefore, there is no unity of the self.

If there is knowledge, there is no error; thus, the conceit of a knower is not admitted. And if there is ignorance, there is no absence of error; thus, the conceit of an ignorant person is not admitted. (70)
Furthermore, because the ether is unchanging and unattached, it is not logical for the Self to possess agency, nor is it logical for it to possess the state of being an enjoyer. (71)
If the self is not the agent, how can the fruit of the action accrue to the agent?
The analogy of the king is not tenable, because the king is a partaker in the sin. (72)

And oneness is not logical for that which is non-dual, because it does not depend on anything external. If it were one by virtue of being joined with oneness, then that [oneness] alone would possess the conjunction, and nothing else. (73)
If unity is established by first conceptualizing multiplicity and then excluding it,
that unity would not exist in reality, because such conceptualization is merely conventional.

If that [object] exists in reality in the form of permanence, unity, and so forth, then the application of words and cognitions such as "one" and so on would be unerring when the object is present. (75)
And since there are conceptual constructions such as "oneness" and so forth, how can it be non-conceptual?
Furthermore, the operation of words is unrestricted regarding an object that is the domain of conceptual construction. (76)
For if it is thus beyond the scope of the intellect, how could it be within the range of words?
Even if it were inexpressible and free from conceptual construction, it would still be unreal, according to the previous reasoning. (77)

If liberation results from seeing [the self] by means of the intellect, then how can there be oneness given their difference? Like the cognition of multiplicity, that [cognition of oneness] would also be false, because it grasps [the object] as it was before. (78)
When gnosis has reached the equality of non-arising, since there is no differentiation, where could there be seeing?
From the absence of seeing, liberation would occur; yet, for no one does liberation exist [as a separate entity]. (79)
If awakening exists because it arises from that [non-arising], how can there be equality through non-arising?
If there is no arising because of the existence of reality, then that too is equal to conceptual construction. (80)
The phenomenon of non-birth is like birth; and even when that [birth] is absent, it exists.
Neither its identity with the self nor its abiding within it is tenable. (81)
What difference is there in the unborn (aja) by which it could be supported through reasoning?
For, in reality, the state of being unborn is not admitted for both that which has been born and that which has not been born. //82//
If its non-difference from a sky-flower is asserted, then you have accepted the position of the non-existent;
if there is a difference in their established nature, then non-duality is not proven. ||83||
Therefore, the Person (puruṣa) is neither an entity nor a non-entity; he is neither distinct nor non-distinct [from them];
he is neither eternal nor non-eternal, and he is not an object of the intellect or of words. ||84||

Since the object of knowledge is not established in any way whatsoever, it is logical that it is beyond the range of the intellect; and when the range of the intellect ceases, it must also be beyond the range of words. ||85||
Considering this auspicious method of the Tathāgata to be unerring, the non-Buddhist teachers, having conceived a longing for it, have likewise composed works on that subject. (86)
Who will have faith in that [teaching] which contradicts itself from beginning to end, like a jewel of a completely different nature compared to iron? (87)
However, due to the diversity of the teaching, this method may be applied here in this way:
for the sake of attracting some, and for the purpose of turning others away from grasping at what remains. (88)
For the non-arising of phenomena is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it is uncontrived;
and because it is indestructible, it is also called the "self" (*ātman*). (89)
It is one because of its uniform nature, and it is non-different even amidst the diversity of entities;
it is all-pervading because it is the nature of all phenomena, and it is eternal because it is indestructible. ||90||
Because it is unborn, this [Self] is unborn; for that very reason, it is free from old age and death.
Because it does not fall away, it is infallible; and because of its excellence, it is considered supreme. (91)
It is not form, sound, smell, and so forth; nor is it earth, fire, water, or wind;
nor is it space, the moon, the sun, and so on; nor does it have the characteristic of mind or cognition. (92)
It is "all" because it is its own intrinsic nature, and it is "not all" because it is indestructible;
therein, due to the non-arising of afflictions and the like, it is both pure and indeed peaceful. (93)
Due to the superimposition of conceptual construction, it is expressible; yet in reality, it is inexpressible.
Because it is inexpressible in every respect, this stainless one is thus described.
If such a self is indeed intended by you as well, then it is faultless and supported by reasoning, owing to its many points of similarity with [the self of] the Nāstikas and others. (95)
For those who are terrified of selflessness itself, their very fear causes them to remain fixed in that very state;
for how could one who is afraid of space find a dwelling anywhere else? (96)
Welcome; let it be made. Here no one is excluded from satisfaction.
This is the supreme nectar of reality belonging to the Buddhas, the kinsmen of the world. (97)
Moreover, let this false grasping—which has no basis and which consists of [the notions of] selfhood, agency, and enjoyership, and which obstructs the vision of reality—be utterly abandoned. (98)
Because they are not born from an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the non-arising of entities is considered their reality in the ultimate sense;
for since they are not born by way of an intrinsic nature, this is said to be their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). (99)
The absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) and selflessness (*nairātmya*) cannot be identical with that [nature], because they are contradictory.
If that which is non-self were the self, then even the absence of a cow would be a cow. (100)
How could this absence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) be consistent with being an agent and an enjoyer?
For agency and enjoyment do not occur spontaneously, as is the case with the son of a barren woman when he is perceived [to have them]. 101.
How can there be birth from such a [non-existent] thing, or how could there be dissolution therein?
It is not logical to conceive of production or dissolution in a sky-flower. (102)

As long as cognition proceeds with respect to the non-existence of intrinsic nature, so long are [concepts] such as "one" and so forth considered to be superimpositions consisting of intellectual construction. (103)
When the intellect, both conceptual and non-conceptual, ceases—within that which is not an object of cognitions, there is the auspicious cessation of phenomenal proliferation. 104.
The eighth chapter, titled "The Entrance into the Determination of the Reality of Vedānta," [ends with the verse]:
"Even a bull would become a cow. (100)

How could this absence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) be consistent with being an agent and an enjoyer? For such things are not seen, just as [agency and enjoyment] are not seen in the son of a barren woman.
The Ninth Chapter: An Introduction to the Determination of the Reality of Mīmāṃsā.
Some are detractors of the meditation and knowledge that constitute the true path to liberation.
Having propounded that its attainment occurs through mere ritual action, they are devoid of shame. ||1||
Based on the scriptures, they say that for one who performs the rites involving rice, animals, clarified butter, and the wife as prescribed by the treatises,
no other path is suitable for attaining liberation.
Because a person's speech is corrupted by defects such as passion and the like, it is false; however, the Veda is accepted as authoritative because it is not authored by a person. ||3||
Because no author is remembered, the Veda is accepted as having no human author;
because its tradition has not been interrupted, it is an authoritative scripture (āgama).
But after that has passed, [it is] ten [days]. ||4||

For how could there be any comprehension of an object that is absolutely beyond the senses—such as heaven, the unseen potency (*apūrva*), and so forth—when its connection with any inferential mark (*liṅga*) has not been perceived? (5)
Sound is eternal, manifested by phonation, and its relationship with the meaning is eternal; for it is from this [relationship] that the cognizer [comprehends it].
Practice arises with respect to the goals. ||6||
Because it arises from two [causes], because of its repeated practice, and likewise because of recognition;
and because sound is audible like [other] sounds, sound is determined to be eternal. (7)
And this [scriptural testimony] is distinct from inference because it is a means of valid cognition, like anything other than that;
or else, it is the apprehension of objects that are either single or multiple. (8)

Because it is the cause of the cognition of an object whose relationship with its inferential mark is unperceived, or else because it is the cause for the arising of a cognition whose object is distinct [from that of perception]. ||9||
Even that which is unprecedented is manifested by action; action is also a means to liberation,
just as a wise man might conquer Death through the drinking of Soma and other rites.

The ancient and auspicious path, honored and cherished by the celestial sages and the wise, which is the triple Veda (trayī), is being abandoned by women and Śūdras who stand outside the meaning of the Vedas. 11.
Whatever exists here is found elsewhere; what does not exist here is not found anywhere.
Even in the case of the fourfold [categories] beginning with *dharma*, that very same thing is seen elsewhere. (12)
Having corrupted the path of the Three Vedas with logical arguments, those proponents of reasoning, because they prioritize inference, illuminate their own system. ||13||
For those who rely primarily on inference, like the blind running on a rugged path by the mere touch of their feet, a fall is not difficult to encounter. (14)
Nor does there exist anyone who is omniscient, since no such person is seen at present;
for the omniscience of a Buddha is merely a conceptual construct intended for the edification of the world. //15//
The word of the Buddha is not authoritative because it is a product, like anything else;
and the Perfectly Awakened One is not omniscient because he is a human being, like anyone else. (16)
The word of the Buddha is not authoritative because it refutes the teachings of the Three Vedas;
whatever is stated [by him] is stated [falsely], just like the doctrine of the naked ascetics (Jainas). ||17||
Therefore, in this matter as well, those who seek the truth as it is—being experts in words, meanings, and logic—investigate while abandoning the poison of partiality. (18)

Since scripture possesses the status of scripture due to the non-interruption of its tradition, and since the status of scripture is thus established for everything [claimed to be such], let it be determined: what is reality? (19)
If a statement is capable of withstanding examination through reasoning, then that alone is scripture;
for it is precisely that which has been uttered [by the Buddha] which must first be investigated. (20)

In that regard, let it be accepted that liberation results from knowledge because it is the antidote to that [ignorance], just as one is freed from disease through medicine because it is the antidote to the malady. (21)
Because it is an action, liberation is not desired as an action, like agriculture;
for [liberation] is denotable while being non-action, or else because it is limited in time. (22)
If it is maintained that human speech is not authoritative because it is corrupted by defects,
then the reason [adduced] would be subject to the fallacy of inconclusiveness (vyabhicāra) due to the words of goldsmiths and the like.
Now, if the authority of the Veda is sought to be established on the grounds of its being authorless,
the reason would be both unestablished and inconclusive. (24)
If [the Buddha] were not the author because of his being a mere restatement (anuvāda), then even a Buddhist [teaching] would be without an author;
for that which was perfectly realized by previous Buddhas is restated by the Buddhas. (25)
Furthermore, because of the inference from the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), there is a sublation of the thesis (*pakṣabādha*) by means of that inference;
and because the non-remembrance of an author is unestablished, the logical reason (*hetu*) would be unproven (*asiddhatā*). ||26||

If that [scripture] were produced by the very same person who previously composed the mantra, or if it were intended as a treatise composed by that same author, then it would be either authored by him or not authored at all. (27)

Why is it that the authorship of the scripture is not likewise perceived, given its simultaneous arising with the author, as in the case of those who compose works by recollecting their past lives? (28)
Whether by way of conformity with practice or through the traditional transmission of phonemes, why is the human authorship of Vedic sentences not accepted? (29)
For this reason as well, the authorship of Vedic sentences by a person is accepted, because they are the cause for the arising of the cognition of the intended meaning, just like a gesture. (30)
And this Veda is to be inferred as having been composed by unworthy persons,
because it teaches actions such as injury to living beings and the drinking of wine, like the scriptures of the Māgas. (31)

If violence, like the administration of poison, were not desired as a giver of undesirable results because it is encompassed by mantras—or even because of scriptural injunctions—then it would be like [the giving of] a gift. (32)

For that which consists of approaching women who should not be approached by means of mantras, aphrodisiacs, powders, and so forth, the former [reason] is inconclusive; and the latter [reason] is [inconclusive] because of the drinking of liquor. (33)
The undertaking of a mantra is intended for the purpose of cutting off life and so forth; it yields undesirable results for the practitioner, like the employment of poison or weapons. (34)
If [the reason] is stated only within one's own treatise, then the "Liberator from Saṃsāra" would be established [as a valid example];
and if the reason is stated in a general way, there would be the fallacy of being unestablished for one of the two parties (anyatarāsiddhatā). (35)
If the killing of animals in a sacrifice does not yield an undesirable result, it is because it is for that purpose;
for just as the act of cooking is accepted when performed for the sake of a Brahmin. (36)
Animals are desired for the sake of being enjoyed by an enjoyer, because they are objects of enjoyment, just like a woman;
therefore, since the purpose of sacrifice is established for animals, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unproven. (37)

And this act of violence performed within the sacrificial altar, because it is intentional and not a mistaken killing, yields an undesirable fruit for the agent in the future, just like any other [sinful act]. (38)

For this reason as well, violence performed in sacrifice is held to yield undesirable results, because it involves the deliberate destruction of life and the infliction of suffering, just like any other [act of violence]. (39)
For whatever kind of result an action produces when its locus is visible,
that same kind of result it produces for the agent even when [the locus] is invisible—
whether it be violence or otherwise. (40)
The drinking of intoxicants and so forth has been explained by means of the aforementioned renunciation:
"Intoxicants should not be consumed because they cause intoxication, just like the thorn-apple (*dhustūra*) and other such plants. (41)
The drinking of intoxicants is not without fault in a sacrifice simply because it is encompassed by mantras;
because it is intoxication, just as elsewhere it is seen [to be faulty] despite being encompassed by mantras. (42)

If it is argued that there is no certainty regarding heaven and so forth because no perceptible mark (liṅga) exists, then why is there not certainty regarding the prover (niścetuḥ), since it too is inferred from a mark? (43)

In the argument "because it does not proceed from two," since this reason is inconclusive even with respect to a lamp— given that a lamp also does not proceed from two— the permanence of sound is likewise untenable. (44)
Because it is existent, why is this sound not understood to be non-eternal like an action?
Or else, because it is the cause of cognition, it must be perishable, like the movement of the body. (45)
The reasons of "repeated practice" and "recognition" lack positive concomitance (anvaya) with respect to repeated practice and recognition in the case of impermanent things.
As is seen in some cases. ||46||
Since the permanence of "sound-ness" (śabdatva) has not been established, "sound-ness" cannot serve as an illustrative example;
furthermore, because manifestation is denied, this [sound] is not something manifested by articulated sounds (dhvani). (47)

If sound (*śabda*) is what you mean by "the audible" (*śrāvaṇa*), how can it be considered manifested by resonance (*dhvani*)? For its comprehension arises from convention (*saṃketa*); thus, it follows that this is merely a word. (48)

Because a linguistic convention is impossible at the beginning, comprehension [of such a convention] is not tenable; for, like cyclic existence, the convention is beginningless and thus functions as a restatement of what already exists. (49)
The status of being a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) in inference is not distinct from its own nature;
therefore, the reason "because it is a means of valid cognition" is stated to be inconclusive (anaikāntika). ||50||
Because it is established that their spheres of operation are distinct, the reason would be unestablished;
nor is the other [reason] [unestablished], since it consists in being the cause for the arising of cognitions with distinct spheres of operation. (51)
Inference is also accepted because it is inseparable from multiple objects;
since it is not a cause for the cognition of a single object, it does not differ from verbal testimony. //52//

Since the understanding of the object to be known arises through inference for the sake of another when the relationship with the mark (liṅga) has not been previously perceived, it is therefore not a different entity [from that inference]. //53//
Verbal cognition is not distinct from inference, because it is a cause of indirect cognition;
for it depends upon the recollection of a relationship, just as inference does by its very nature. //54//
Nor can it be something previously non-existent manifested by an action, as in the case of the negation of the manifestation of a word;
or rather, like a jar, let the previously non-existent be accepted as impermanent due to its manifestation. (55)
It is held that the fruit of actions such as drinking soma is impermanent;
because it is the fruit of an action, it is not desired as a fruit resulting from desire or a specific occasion. (56)

The practice of drinking soma and so forth is not logically capable of bringing about liberation, because it is a ritual action; just as, for example, ritual actions performed for the sake of desire or on specific occasions are not so regarded. ||57||
Therefore, one who has taken recourse to this path does not conquer Death; for this path is favored by those led by others, whose intellects are incapable of discernment. (58)
Having observed that the conduct of Brahmā, Keśava, and Śūlin— the founders of the path of the three Vedas— is characterized by affliction, it is fitting that the Trayī be abandoned.
Through knowledge, the wise burn away their sin just as fire consumes fuel;
therefore, due to that particular intensity of splendor, they are not subject to misfortune.
The wise know that knowledge to be true knowledge which is capable of burning away the afflictions;
therefore, the knower does not commit sin, because the cause for it no longer exists.
"One who possesses the yoga of perfection is not stained by action or by sin"—by those speaking thus, having strayed from the true path, others too have been led astray. (62)
The intellect that perceives the true nature of reality is not admitted to exist in Brahmā and the others;
for how could Brahmā and the Trident-bearer (Śiva) both be so passionately enamored with Tilottamā? (63)
How did he, who was previously not consumed by the fire of his own wrath, burn the triple city (Tripura), and why did he punish the teeth of Pūṣan and the eyes of Bhaga? (64)

If even a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, or a lustful man becomes a Lord once he has perceived the Truth, what need is there to speak of those who have perceived the Truth and follow his path? 65.
And how did Keśava, out of cruelty, deprive Keśin, Cāṇūra, Naraka, and the others of their lives and their virtues? (66)
One who takes the wives and wealth of others, a drinker of intoxicants, and a destroyer of living beings—if such a person has seen Hari, then victory belongs to the Śabaras and the thieves! (67)
Because he is skilled in protecting the subjects, there is no fault in his slaying the asuras, who are thorns to the gods,
provided it is for the sake of guarding dharma.
The taking of another's wife or wealth, and the practice of deceit and hypocrisy—have these not been abandoned [by him], if he indeed desires the protection of Dharma? (69)

If unrighteousness belongs to the senses and not to him [the Lord], how can he be the agent of creation? Or rather, was his creation brought about by defects of unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa) due to ignorance? ||70||
Does he protect the world out of craving, or how can one who is a slave to craving be a capable agent?
If it is out of compassion, then why did he delude the world with illusion as if it were ordinary magic? (71)
Why would there be no compassion for the asuras, who suffer from death, birth, and so forth?
Because he perceives equality everywhere, it is not appropriate for him to have the notion of "enemy. (72)
How can such conduct, variegated with passion, hatred, and the like, belong to Hari?
And how can he who acts in such an ignoble manner be the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)? ||73||
If that auspicious form of Hari is conceived as something other [than his true nature], then even ascetics, having seen it, do not return to rebirth. (74)
She is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is she considered both existent and non-existent;
therefore, because of her existence, non-existence, and both existence and non-existence, she is supreme.
If she were different from the forms such as Matsya and others, then because of that difference, she would not be Acyuta (the Imperishable);
yet, because she is non-different, she is not other than them either—yet she too is unpeaceful, just like the other.
Moreover, if one part of that single self were unpeaceful while another part were peaceful,
she would be called a "prostitute," even though she is virtuous and restrained by half of her body.
It is not tenable to say that [the Self] is "supreme" (parā) because it cannot be denoted by words such as "existent" (sat);
for supremacy is appropriate only for that which exists, and likewise, causality is appropriate for it. (78)

Because its causality is rejected and because it is other [than the cause] as previously stated, it is neither a cause nor is it something else; furthermore, it is not "acyuta" (imperishable) because it is unborn. //79//
If the Imperishable (acyuta) were a positive entity (bhāva), it would be subject to destruction, like taste and other such qualities.
If the Imperishable were a non-entity (abhāva), it would be non-existent, like a flower in the sky. ||80||
Thus, existence and non-existence are not logical, just as heat and cold cannot coexist in fire;
furthermore, if it were inexpressible, how could it be the immutable (acyuta)? ||81||
Nor is it inexpressible like the self, because that [self] is negated;
for if there were no one who does not fall away due to non-falling, then one who does not fall away would not be "non-falling. (82)
And as for that other form of his which was fashioned to conceal his vices—how can those who desire liberation be freed while clinging to it? (83)
Withdrawing the senses from their objects like a tortoise drawing in its limbs,
if one who is devoted to Him utters the syllable *oṃ* with mindfulness, he is liberated. (84)

Liberation is not possible for those devoted to Hari through the vision of Hari, because it involves conceptualization and recollection, just as [it is not possible] from the vision of Hari [in that sense]. (85)
Even non-conceptual cognition is not desired for the liberation of one engaged in yoga, because it involves the grasping of signs; how much more so, then, that which is purely imagined? (86)
Because of the manifestation of passion and other afflictions, Brahmā and the others are like Kirātas;
having set aside the investigation of reality, there can be no doubt regarding the cause. (87)
The protection of the Dharma may occur either through the teaching of the true Dharma or through one's own practice; yet in both these ways, it is difficult to maintain among these [beings]. (88)
And all [these systems] individually assert that their own self is the cause of creation;
among these, whose word should be considered true and whose false? (89)

If it is argued that there is no fault because of their oneness, then how could even Brahmā be a killer of a Brahmin? Furthermore, since oneness is negated, that [notion of] oneness is illogical. Moreover, since [the three] are distinct selves, [their identity] is impossible; thus, how could there be a triad of rulers?
For those who are deluded regarding the cause of suffering, what need is there for talk about the means to its pacification? (91)
Because their teachings on the Vedas, yoga, and so forth are incomplete, they are not capable of protecting the Dharma by means of proclaiming the true Dharma. (92)
And because they are themselves deficient in the practice, they are not able to lead others to peace, just as a guide who has fallen into a precipice cannot lead others along his own path. (93)

In the Triple Veda, that which is investigated by those whose reasoning is perverted—constructed through a web of conceptualization—is logically inconsistent; yet that which is consistent with logic is abandoned in the Triple Veda. (94)
It was stated previously that it is logical for the universe to have Īśvara and others as its cause; yet, even if Īśvara and others were the creators, what indeed could be produced by them? (95)
First of all, because the self is unproduced, it is not accepted as being created by that [action];
nor are merit and demerit accepted as belonging to it, since they are its qualities, just as they are now. (96)
The body, too, is produced from those two for the sake of experiencing pleasure and pain;
therefore, the body of embodied beings is not rightly held to have God or any other as its creator. (97)

At the beginning of a kalpa, the body of embodied beings arises from the cause of previously performed karma (adṛṣṭa), because it is the cause for the production of pleasure and so forth, just like the present body. ||98||
If the sovereignty of the Lord were produced by merit, then, because he would be dependent upon that merit, the Lord would be a non-Lord. (99)
If it is maintained that the sovereignty of the Lord is without cause, then because it is common to others as well, he would be a non-Lord. (100)
If the Lord is conscious by nature, then the world created by him must be conscious;
for since everything conforms to its cause, your entire world would be sentient. (101)

If God were the cause, the world would be like the power of atomization (*aṇimā*) and the other [siddhis]; or else, if the world is not like the power of atomization and the others, then God would not be the cause. (102)

If the Lord were the agent of karma, he too would be cooked in the hells; or else, in the ripening of others' karma, there would be the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done. (103)
And since the cause of suffering is eternal, how could that suffering be pacified? For the subsiding of heat is never seen while the fire continues to blaze. (104)
How can there be a diversity of effects from that which is itself unitary and undifferentiated?
Nor is it logical for a single entity to possess diversity due to the diversity of [auxiliary factors] such as desire. (105)
"It is said that the cause of the universe is eternal, partless, subtle, one, and all-pervading; what else could be more wonderful than that? (106)
If it were for the sake of sport or for that purpose, then its fruit would indeed be pleasure;
yet because pleasure depends upon oneself or another, the Lord would become a non-Lord. (107)
By animals who fear devouring one another and find festivals rare, and even by those in hell tormented by sufferings such as crushing, cutting, and burning; (108)
Salutations to that Rudra, whose name is true to its meaning, who is pleased by men afflicted by the exhaustion of birth, old age, disease, fear, and sorrow. 109.
That miserly men possess wealth, or that those who subsist on the food of others are endowed with sattva, or that some unrighteous people dwell in heaven—this is clearly the sport of the Lord. (110)
Those with short lifespans possess the wealth of virtue, while those who live long are of wicked conduct;
and those who give are of meager means—this is clearly the work of the Lord.
For some Buddhists are happy while their devotees are miserable;
and by the decree of the Lord's command, why would the evildoer not be a partaker of merit? (112)
The ignorant one is said to be the cause of the diversity of karma;
by this, the creatorship of Brahmā and Kṛṣṇa regarding creation is refuted. (113)
Having restrained the gateway of the mind and fixed the intellect upon Śiva,
one should meditate upon the syllable Om while maintaining concentration within the heart.

The claim that "one whose mind was previously concentrated through the practice of meditative concentration on earth and other elements reaches the end of suffering when the Lord is pleased" is also untrue.
As long as the arising of agreeable cognition persists, liberation is not tenable;
just as liberation is not tenable prior to the arising of agreeable cognition. ||116||

Liberation is not possible for those devoted to Īśvara through the perception of a post, because they abide in [the realm of] objective apprehension, just as [liberation is not attained] from the perception of a post. ||117||
If God were the cause of suffering, then because of His eternity, He would be beyond remedy;
therefore, for no one is there an end to suffering through God. (118)

By this, the remaining proponents of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Self are refuted; for, due to its lack of logical consistency, the intellect does not settle upon Īśvara and the others as the object of devotion. ||119||
Seeing that the washing away of sins with water, as well as the buying and selling of auspicious items and the like,
are improperly prescribed in the three Vedas, it is right that the Trayī (the three Vedas) itself be abandoned.
Sin is not washed away by water that has not been touched [by ritual action], because this is unobserved;
nor by mere moistening, because it merely deposits a latent impression (vāsanā), like memory, knowledge, virtue, and so forth. (121)
Neither water from lotuses nor that of the Gaṅgā and other rivers causes one to fall into sin,
because they merely touch or moisten, like the pus flowing from a house.

When previously committed non-virtuous karmas are exhausted through immersion in water and other such means, there shall be no causeless suffering for those who have performed ablutions at sacred fords (tīrtha). 123.
Nor is it the case that upon the exhaustion of karma no one would become a sinner;
if you argue that "the inner self is purified by water," that too is incorrect. (124)
It is held that evil does not transfer to another continuum, because, being formless, it is like the non-transferability of passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth. (125)
It is certain that the giving and receiving of merit and so forth are not logical, because they are associated with the mind, just as is the case with pleasure and pain. ||126||
Having seen that the Veda prescribes such ill-conceived acts as going to the world of Brahmā and so forth by means of falling into fire and the like, it is proper that the Triple Veda be abandoned.
Jumping into fire or off a precipice is not the cause for attaining the world of Brahmā and so forth,
because it results in the destruction of life, like the act of jumping onto a moth or similar insect.
The renunciation of food and drink is not held to be a means for attaining heaven, because it is a cause of suffering such as hunger, just like fasting performed against one's will. (129)

Just as merit arises from fasting and the like, and the cessation of evil from renunciation, so too would there be such deviation [of the reason] due to causes such as truthfulness and renunciation. (130)

The renunciation of enjoyment does not lead to merit, since this action is free from fault, just as the mental attention of one whose mind is auspicious is like having abandoned mental attention. //131//
Meat that is pure in three respects is not a cause of sin when eaten,
because it has been transformed into bodily fluids and so forth, just as alms-food is not a cause of sin.
Meat is not eaten for the purpose of eating, because it is a cause of evil;
rather, it is consumed as a means to counteract hunger, like food obtained by chance. (133)
If meat is not to be eaten because of its impurity, then consider the body as well:
it is impure by virtue of its origin from the seed and its subsequent nourishment, just like excrement or a worm. (134)
Fish and meat are censured precisely because they originate from semen and other such substances;
yet, since [these substances] are also the cause for ghee, milk, and so forth, there would thus be a logical inconsistency.
If it is held that one who eats meat is a killer of living beings because [the eating] is caused by that [killing],
then for this reason, the argument would be subject to the fallacy of inconclusiveness (vyabhicāra) on account of those who wear skins and so forth.

The consumption of meat is not sinful at that time, because it does not cause suffering to living beings, just like the use of rice and water from which the peacock feathers and other parts have been removed. (137)
Because passion arises from mental construction (*saṃkalpa*), the eating of meat is not its cause;
for it arises even without that, as in the case of grass-eating cows. (138)
Having seen that consciousness has been attributed to insentient and immobile things—a poorly formulated doctrine within the Triple Veda—it is proper that the Triple Veda be abandoned. 139.
For trees do not possess consciousness, because they are not included within the four modes of birth;
moreover, even when cut through the middle, they lack movement, and thus, being insentient, they are like a clod of earth.

If, through contact, there is contraction—as in the case of a *maṇḍalakārikā*—then the same applies to those who possess consciousness, such as those who perform the *samaṅga* and *añjalikārika* gestures. (141)
The reason would be inconclusive due to cases such as hair that has been touched by fire, or especially due to hair mixed with powder or mercury. (142)
For trees cannot be considered sentient beings because they are subject to medical treatment;
furthermore, there is doubt [regarding their permanence] because even substances like wine, once destroyed, may return to existence. (143)

Because they produce offspring of their own kind, because they grow, because they experience longing, because they are born in season, and because they sleep, [plants] possess consciousness; they are not desired [to be insentient], unlike horses and the like. (144)
Because of the presence of exceptions—such as ringworm, coral, lapis lazuli, hair, and golden sprouts—trees are not established as being endowed with consciousness. (145)

Precisely because these [trees] lack consciousness, their [alleged] reasons—such as the presence of pregnancy-longings (*dohada*) and so forth—are unestablished in their meaning; furthermore, they are inconclusive due to [the occurrence of such phenomena] in diseases. (146)

By the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, trees and other things arise according to the time, such as the weapons-trees and jewel-trees in hell and the heavenly world respectively. (147)
For the path of the Three Vedas is indeed true to its meaning, as stated by Brahmā, just like the science of medicine and so forth;
or if it is established on the grounds that it was spoken by those who know the past and the future. (148)
The ninth chapter, titled "The Entrance into the Determination of the Reality of Investigation," [concerning] sandalwood,
lapis lazuli, hair, golden sprouts, and so forth.
However, because of the occurrence of deviation, trees are not established as being endowed with consciousness. ||145||
Because they are devoid of mind, desires and so forth are not established for them;
thus ends the tenth chapter,
the "Instruction on the Proof of the Omniscient One."
Seeing it thus, the Teacher did not prevent him from going forth. ||13||
Beholding the miracles and listening to his teaching, and observing the accumulation of merit of Sunakṣatra, [the Buddha] maintained [his presence]. ||14||
The tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Proof of Omniscience.
The eleventh chapter.
The Exposition of the Characteristics of Praise:

Desiring to lead the world—which is utterly deluded even in its conventional dealings and obscured by a multitude of views—toward the non-dual reality that is like space, [the author] intends to bring forth the spiritual fitness of sentient beings. (1)
Homage to that Knower of the World, who for the benefit of both worlds has taught the true worldly convention as well as that which transcends the world. (2)
Thus, this *Heart of the Middle Way* has been composed in brief;
it is a mirror for the wise to behold the reflections of the many *sūtrāntas*. (3)
Whatever merit has been gained from correctly explaining this treatise, the *Madhyamakahṛdaya*, [I dedicate it].
Whatever I may attain for even a moment, by that may all beings become vessels for enlightenment. //4//
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Characteristics of Praise," is concluded.
The *Tarkajvālā* treatise is finished. [The author] desires to lead the world toward the non-dual reality, which is like space, by means of the spiritual fitness of sentient beings. (1)
Homage to that Knower of the World, who for the benefit of both worlds has taught the true worldly convention as well as that which transcends the world. (2)
Thus, this *Heart of the Middle Way* has been composed in brief;
it is a mirror for the wise to behold the reflections of the many sūtras. (3)
Whatever merit has been gained from correctly explaining this treatise on the *Madhyamaka-hṛdaya*, may it [be dedicated].
By whatever I have attained for even a moment, may all beings become vessels for enlightenment. //4//
